In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those who stand in ranks,﴾ ﴿and those who drive away with a driving,﴾ ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ ﴿indeed your God is One,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr and Hamza recited ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ with idgham (assimilation, the merging of one letter into the next) of the tā' into the letter that follows it, and likewise in His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ and ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾. The rest recited with idhhar (clear pronunciation, without merging). Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The idgham of the tā' into the ṣād is good because the two letters are close in articulation. Do you not see that both are produced from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the front teeth, and both are heard in the whispered sound? The letter into which it is merged exceeds the merged letter in emphasis (iṭbāq) and sibilance (ṣafīr). The merging of the lesser into the greater is good, but it is not permissible for the greater in sound to be merged into the lesser. Also, the idgham of the tā' into the zāy in His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ is good, because the tā' is voiceless (mahmūsah) and the zāy is voiced (majhūrah), and in it there is an increase of sibilance as there was in the ṣād. Also, the idgham of the tā' into the dhāl in His saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ is good, because the two agree in being produced from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the front teeth. As for the one who recited with idhhar and left out the idgham, that is due to the difference in points of articulation (makhārij). And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Regarding these three things by which Allah swears, it is possible that they are three attributes of one subject, and it is possible that they are three distinct things. As for the first possibility, there are several opinions:

The first: They are attributes of the angels, and the meaning is that the angels stand in rows. Either in the heavens to perform worship, as Allah reported about them that they said: ﴿And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks﴾ [As-Saffat 37:165]. It was also said that they align their wings in the air, standing and awaiting the arrival of the command of Allah to them. It is also possible to say that the meaning of their being in ranks is that each of them has a specific station and a specific degree in nobility and virtue, or in essence and loftiness, and that degree, being ordered, remains unchanged, and this resembles rows.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾, al-Layth said: It is said, "I drove the camel (zajartu al-ba'ir), so I drive it (azjuruhu) with a driving," when you urge it to go forward. And, "I drove so-and-so away from evil, and he was driven off (fa-nzajara)," meaning, I forbade him, and he desisted. So, according to this, driving a camel is like urging, and driving a person is like forbidding. Having understood this, we say that there are several views on describing the angels with driving:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: It refers to the angels entrusted with the clouds, who drive them, meaning that they bring them from one place to another.

The second: What is meant is that the angels have influences upon the hearts of the children of Adam by way of inspirations, so they drive them away from sins with a driving.

The third: Perhaps the angels also drive the devils away from harming the children of Adam with evil and injury. I say: It has been established in the rational sciences that existent things are of three categories: an agent that does not accept an effect, and this is Allah, glorified and exalted, who is the noblest of existent things; a recipient that does not act, and these are the world of bodies, which are the lowliest of existent things; and an existent that acts upon something and is acted upon by something else, and this is the world of spirits. This is because they receive the effect from the world of the majesty of Allah, and then they act upon the world of bodies. Know that the aspect by which they receive the effect from the world of the majesty of Allah is other than the aspect by which they dominate the world of bodies and are able to manage it. His saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ points to the most noble aspect by which they are able to influence the world of bodies. Having understood this, His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ points to their standing in rows, row after row, in the station of servitude and obedience, with humility and submission. This is the aspect by which those holy substances receive the kinds of divine lights and eternal perfections. His exalted saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ points to the influence of the angelic substances in illuminating the holy human spirits and bringing them from potentiality to actuality. This is because it has been established that these human rational spirits, in relation to the spirits of the angels, are like a drop in relation to the sea and like a spark in relation to the sun. And that these human spirits, in relation to the spirits of the angels, are like a drop in relation to the sea and like a spark in relation to the sun. And that these human spirits move from potentiality to actuality in divine knowledge and spiritual perfections only through the influences of the angelic substances. A parallel to this is His exalted saying: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [An-Nahl 16:2], and His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down ﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 26:193–194], and His exalted saying: ﴿And those who bring the reminder﴾ [Al-Mursalat 77:5]. Having understood this, we say that there is another subtle point in this verse, which is that absolute perfection of a thing is achieved only when it is complete and beyond complete. By being complete is meant that all the perfections befitting it are attained in actuality, and by being beyond complete is meant that kinds of perfections and felicities overflow from it onto others. It is known that being perfect in itself precedes being a perfecter of others. Having understood this, His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ points to the perfecting of the angelic substances in their essences at the time they stand in stations of servitude and rows of service and obedience. His exalted saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ points to the manner of their influence in removing what is unbecoming from the substances of human spirits. His exalted saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ points to the manner of their influence in pouring holy manifestations and divine lights upon the human rational spirits. These are rational correspondences and true considerations to which these three words apply.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: It is not permissible to apply these words to the angels, because they imply femininity, and the angels are free of this attribute. The answer is in two respects:

The first: that ﴿aṣ-ṣāffāt﴾ is a plural of a plural, for it is said: a feminine group (jamā'ah ṣāffah), then it is pluralized as ṣāffāt.

The second: that they are free of semantic femininity, but as for feminine form in the wording, that is not so. And how could it be, when they are called angels (malā'ikah), although the sign of the feminine is present in this form?

The second: That these ṣāffāt may be understood as the pure, holy human souls that devote themselves to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, who are the angels of the earth. Its explanation is in two respects:

The first aspect: that His exalted saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ means the rows formed when prayers are performed in congregation,

*Page 102*

and His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ points to the recitation of "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan," as if by reciting this phrase they drive the devils away from casting whisperings into their hearts during prayer. And His saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ points to the recitation of the Qur'an in prayer. It was also said: ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ points to raising the voice in recitation, as if one drives away Satan by means of raising the voice. It was narrated that he (ﷺ) went around the houses of his companions at night, and he heard Abu Bakr reciting in a low voice, and he heard 'Umar reciting in a loud voice. He asked Abu Bakr: "Why do you recite like this?" He said: "The One Worshipped is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." And he asked 'Umar: "Why do you recite like this?" He said: "I wake the sleeper and drive away the devil."

The second aspect: Regarding the interpretation of these three words in this verse, what is meant by His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ is the rows formed by the scholars who are upright and who call to the religion of Allah, exalted is He. What is meant by His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ is their occupation with driving away from doubts and desires. What is meant by His exalted saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ is their occupation with calling to the religion of Allah and encouraging acting upon the laws of Allah.

The third aspect: Regarding the interpretation of these three words, we may apply them to the states of warriors and fighters in the cause of Allah. His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ means the battle lines, in accordance with His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks﴾ [As-Saff 61:4]. As for ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾, the zajrah and the ṣayḥah (outcry) are the same, and what is meant is raising the voice in driving the horses. As for ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾, what is meant is the occupation of the fighters, at the time they begin battling the enemy, with reciting the Qur'an and remembering Allah, exalted is He, by saying the tahlil (there is no god but Allah) and tasbih and taqdis (glorification and sanctification).

It was narrated that he (ﷺ) went around the houses of his companions at night, and he heard Abu Bakr reciting in a low voice, and he heard 'Umar reciting in a loud voice. He asked Abu Bakr: "Why do you recite like this?" He said: "The One Worshipped is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." And he asked 'Umar: "Why do you recite like this?" He said: "I wake the sleeper and drive away the devil."

The second aspect: Regarding the interpretation of these three words in this verse, what is meant by His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ is the rows formed by the scholars who are upright and who call to the religion of Allah, exalted is He. What is meant by His saying ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾ is their occupation with driving away from doubts and desires. What is meant by His exalted saying ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾ is their occupation with calling to the religion of Allah and encouraging acting upon the laws of Allah.

The third aspect: Regarding the interpretation of these three words, we may apply them to the states of warriors and fighters in the cause of Allah. His saying ﴿wa-s-saffati saffan﴾ means the battle lines, in accordance with His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks﴾ [As-Saff 61:4]. As for ﴿fa-z-zajirati zajran﴾, the zajrah and the ṣayḥah (outcry) are the same, and what is meant is raising the voice in driving the horses. As for ﴿fa-t-taliyati dhikran﴾, what is meant is the occupation of the fighters, at the time they begin battling the enemy, with reciting the Qur'an and remembering Allah, exalted is He, by saying the tahlil (there is no god but Allah) and tasbih and taqdis (glorification and sanctification).

**Fourth aspect:** On interpreting these three terms, we may take them as attributes of the verses of the Qur'an. So His saying, ﴿By those arrayed in ranks﴾, refers to the verses of the Qur'an, for they are of various kinds: some concern the proofs of Divine Unity (tawhid), some the proofs of His knowledge, power and wisdom, some the proofs of prophethood, some the proofs of the Return (ma'ad, the afterlife), some the explanation of the legal obligations (taklif, the duties imposed on people) and rulings, and some the teaching of noble morals. These verses are arranged in an order that never changes or alters, so these verses resemble persons standing in fixed rows. His saying, ﴿By those that drive away with a driving﴾, refers to the verses that restrain from reprehensible deeds. His saying, ﴿By those that recite the reminder﴾, refers to the verses that indicate the obligation to undertake acts of righteousness and goodness. He described the verses as recited in the manner of what is said: the poetry of a poet and the speech of a speaker. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra: 9], and He said: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Ya Sin: 1–2]. It has been said that "the Wise" (al-Hakim) means "the Judge" (al-Hakim). This is the sum of the possible aspects when these three terms are taken as attributes of one single thing.

As for the second possibility, namely that these three refer to different things: it has been said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿By those arrayed in ranks﴾, is the birds, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the birds in ranks﴾ [al-Nur: 41]; "﴿those that drive away﴾" is everything that restrains from the disobedience of Allah; and "﴿those that recite the reminder﴾" is everything that is recited from the Book of Allah. I say there is another aspect in this matter, namely that the creatures of Allah are either corporeal (jismaniyyah) or spiritual (ruhaniyyah). As for the corporeal, they are arranged in layers and degrees that never change at all. The earth is the center of the world, enclosed by the sphere of water; the water is enclosed by the air; the air is enclosed by the fire; then these four are enclosed by the spheres of the celestial orbs, to the end of the corporeal world. Thus these bodies are as though they were rows standing on the threshold of the majesty of Allah, exalted is He. As for the spiritual substances, they, despite the differences of their degrees and the variety of their attributes, share two qualities:

The first: influence over the world of bodies through moving and directing them, and to this refers His saying, ﴿By those that drive away with a driving﴾. We have already explained that what is meant by this driving is urging and moving.

The second:

**[Page 103]**

perception and total absorption in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and in praising Him. To this refers His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those that recite the reminder﴾. Since the body is lower in rank than the independent spirits, the management of corporeal things is lower in rank than the spirits absorbed in knowing the majesty of Allah and devoted to glorifying Allah, as He said: ﴿And those with Him are not too proud to worship Him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 19]. Therefore, He began at the first rank with mention of the bodies, saying: ﴿By those arrayed in ranks﴾. Then, at the second rank, He mentioned the spirits that govern the bodies of this world. Then, at this third rank, He mentioned the highest degree, which is the holy spirits, wholly turned toward knowing the majesty of Allah and absorbed in praising Him. These are possibilities that have come to mind, and none knows the secrets of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, except Allah.

**Third issue:** On this point people hold two opinions.

The first: the view of those who say that the one sworn by here is the Creator of these things, not the very essences of these things. They argued for this with several arguments:

The first: that he (ﷺ) forbade swearing by other than Allah, so how is it fitting for the wisdom of Allah that He would swear by other than Allah?

The second: that swearing by a thing in such a context is a great exaltation of the one sworn by, and such great exaltation is fitting only for Allah.

The third: that what we have mentioned is reinforced by what He, exalted is He, stated in some surahs, namely His saying: ﴿By the sky and He who built it, by the earth and He who spread it, by the soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 5–7].

The second opinion: the view of those who say that the oath is indeed sworn by the very essences of these things. They argued for this with several arguments.

The first: that the oath was sworn by these things according to the apparent wording, so departing from it is contrary to the evidence.

The second: that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾, so He attached the oath to the sky, then conjoined to it an oath by the Builder of the sky. Had the oath by the sky meant an oath by the One who built the sky, it would entail repetition in one place, and that is not permissible.

The third: that it is not far-fetched that the wisdom behind Allah, exalted is He, swearing by these things is to draw attention to the nobility of their essences and the perfection of their realities, especially if we take these terms to refer to the angels. For then the wisdom in swearing by them is to draw attention to the lofty status of their ranks and the perfection of their stations. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: mention of the oath in this context is not fitting, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: the purpose of this oath is either to establish this claim for the believer or for the unbeliever. The first is invalid, because the believer already affirms it whether or not an oath is made; so this oath is useless under every assumption.

The second: He, exalted is He, swore at the beginning of this surah that the God is one, and He swore at the beginning of the surah al-Dhariyat that the Resurrection is true, saying: ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1], up to His saying: ﴿What you are promised is surely true, and the judgment is surely to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 5–6]. And establishing these lofty and noble claims against opponents such as the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator and the afterlife) and their like by means of oath and solemn assertion is not fitting for intelligent people. The answer has several aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, established Divine Unity and the validity of the Resurrection and the Return in the rest of the surahs by certain proofs. Since the mention of those proofs has already preceded, it is not far-fetched to restate them. So He mentioned the oath as an emphasis on what preceded, especially since the Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and establishing claims by oath and solemn assertion is a familiar method among the Arabs.

The second aspect of the answer: when He, exalted is He, swore by these things concerning the truth of His saying, ﴿Indeed your God is surely one﴾, He followed it with what is like a certain proof that the God is one, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts﴾. This is because He, exalted is He, made clear in His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22] that the orderly arrangement of the conditions of the heavens and the earth indicates that the God is one. So here, when He said: ﴿Indeed your God is surely one﴾, He followed it with: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts﴾, as if it were said: We have made clear that consideration of the orderly arrangement of this world indicates that the God is one; so reflect upon that proof so that knowledge of Divine Unity may be attained by you.

The third aspect of the answer: that the purpose of this speech is a refutation of the idol-worshippers in their claim that the idols are gods. So it is as if it were said: this doctrine has reached such depths of collapse and feebleness that such an argument suffices to refute it. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth issue:** As for the indication of the conditions of the heavens and the earth to the existence of the God who is Powerful, Knowing and Wise, and to His being one, exalted above having a partner, this has already been established in this book many times and in various ways. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and Lord of the easts﴾, it may be that what is meant is the risings of the sun. Al-Suddi said: there are three hundred and sixty easts, and likewise three hundred and sixty wests, for the sun rises every day from one east and sets every day in one west. It may also be that what is meant is the risings of the stars, since every star has an east and a west. If it is asked: why did He mention only the easts? We say, for two reasons:

The first: He mentioned only the easts, as in His saying: ﴿that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81].

The second: the east is stronger in state than the setting and more beneficial than the setting, so the east was mentioned as an alert to the abundance of Allah's kindness toward His servants. And for this subtle point, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, argued by the east, saying: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

[p. 105]

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾ ﴿and as a protection from every rebellious devil﴾ ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side﴾ ﴿driven away, and for them is a constant punishment﴾ ﴿except one who snatches a fragment, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾.

There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, Hafs (on the authority of ʿAsim) recited *zīnatin* with tanwin and *al-kawākibi* in the genitive (jarr). This is the reading of Masruq ibn al-Ajdaʿ. Al-Farrāʾ said: this is the replacement of a definite noun by an indefinite one, as in His saying ﴿bi-l-nāṣiyati, nāṣiyatin﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 15-16], where an indefinite noun is returned to a definite one. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-kawākib* is an apposition (badal) for *al-zīnah*, because it is that very thing, just as you say: "I passed by Abū ʿAbd Allāh Zayd."

ʿAsim recited *al-zīnah* with tanwin and *al-kawākiba* in the accusative. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means "We adorned the stars." Al-Zajjāj said: it is permissible that *al-kawākib* in the accusative be an apposition for His saying ﴿bi-zīnatin﴾, since ﴿bi-zīnatin﴾ is in the accusative position. The rest of the readers recited *bi-zīnati al-kawākibi* in the genitive, by way of idafa (construct phrase).

**The second issue:** God, exalted is He, has declared that He adorned the lowest heaven, and has stated that He adorned it for two benefits:

The first: obtaining adornment.

The second: protection from the rebellious devil. Therefore, we must examine what is said about these three matters.

As for the first:

[p. 106 ends here — no; this is p. 105 continuing] It is the adornment of the lowest heaven with these stars. One may say: it has been established in ʿilm al-hayʾah (astronomy/cosmology) that these fixed stars are set in the eighth sphere, and that the six planets are set in the six spheres that surround the lowest heaven. So how is His saying correct: ﴿Indeed, We adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾?

The answer: people living on the surface of the sphere of the earth, when they look at the sky, see it adorned with these stars. Moreover, we have already explained in ʿilm al-hayʾah that the philosophers have not completed a proof showing that these stars are set in the eighth heaven. Perhaps we explained this matter in the commentary on the surah ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk: 1], in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

As for the second matter, namely that these stars are the adornment of the lowest heaven, it contains two discussions:

**The first discussion:** *al-zīnah* is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like *al-nisbah*, and also a noun for that with which something is adorned, as *al-līqah* is a noun for that with which the inkwell is smeared. The author of al-Kashshāf said: His saying ﴿bi-zīnati al-kawākib﴾ allows both. If you intend the verbal noun, then its idafa is to the agent, meaning that its adornment is the stars; or its idafa is to the object, meaning that God adorned the stars and beautified them, because the heaven was only adorned by their goodness in themselves. If you intend the noun, then the idafa has two possibilities: that *al-kawākib* is an explanation (bayān) of *al-zīnah*, since adornment may be achieved by stars and by other things; or that it means that with which the stars are adorned.

**The second discussion:** In explaining how the stars are an adornment for the heaven, there are several aspects:

The first: light and radiance are among the best and most perfect attributes. When these shining, illuminating stars are present on the surface of the heaven, the light and radiance remain in the body of the heaven because of the presence of these stars in it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: ﴿bi-zīnati al-kawākib﴾ means "with the light of the stars."

The second aspect: it is possible that what is meant is their varied, harmonious shapes, such as the shape of Orion (al-Jawzāʾ), the Bears (Banāt Naʿsh), the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā), and others.

The third aspect: it is possible that what is meant by this adornment is the manner of their rising and setting.

The fourth aspect: when a person in a dark night looks at the surface of the heaven and sees these luminous jewels shining, sparkling and glittering on that blue surface, there is no doubt that they are the best and most perfect of things in composition and substance, and all of this shows that these stars are an adornment.

As for the third matter, namely His saying ﴿and as a protection from every rebellious devil﴾, it contains two discussions:

**The first discussion** concerns language. His saying ﴿wa-ḥifẓan﴾ ("and as a protection") means "and We protected it." Al-Mubarrad said: when you mention a verb and then conjoin to it the verbal noun (maṣdar) of another verb, you put the verbal noun in the accusative, because it indicates its verb. Like your saying: *af'alu wa-karāmatan* ("I will do it, and [out of] honor"); because when he said *af'alu* ("I will do"), it was understood that nouns are not conjoined to verbs, so the meaning is: "I will do that, and I will honor you with honor." Ibn ʿAbbās said: He means the protection of the heaven by the stars. And ﴿min kulli shayṭānin mārid﴾ means: the one who rebelled against God. It has been said: it is the one who cannot be overpowered (lā yutamakkanu minhu), and its root is from smoothness (al-malāsah); from this comes His saying ﴿a palace of smooth glass (ṣarḥun mumarrad)﴾ [al-Naml: 44], and from it comes *al-amrad* (the beardless youth). We have mentioned the explanation of *al-mārid* at His saying ﴿they persisted in hypocrisy (marradū ʿalā al-nifāq)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101].

**The second discussion** concerns the rational questions in this place. We say: the full investigation of this is mentioned at His saying: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. The exegetes said: the devils used to ascend near the heaven, and perhaps they would hear the speech of the angels and thereby learn of the unseen events that would occur, and they would inform people of them, giving the impression that they knew the unseen. So God, exalted is He, prevented them from ascending near the heaven with these meteors (shuhub), for He throws them with them and burns them with them. There remain here several questions:

**[p. 106]**

**The first question:** Are these meteors among the stars with which God adorned the heaven or not? The first is false, because these meteors vanish and disappear. If these meteors were those true stars, then a large decrease in the numbers of the stars of the heaven would have to appear. It is known that this did not happen at all, for the numbers of the stars of the heaven remain in one state without any change whatsoever. Also, making them missiles against the devils necessarily causes a deficiency in the adornment of the heaven, so combining these two purposes is like a contradiction.

As for the second division, namely that one says these meteors are a different kind from the stars set in the sphere, this too is problematic, because He, exalted is He, said in the surah ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk: 1], ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. The pronoun in His saying ﴿wa-jaʿalnāhā﴾ ("and We made them") refers back to the lamps, so those lamps must themselves be the missiles, with their very same essences and without any difference. The answer: these meteors are other than those enduring piercing stars.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾, we say: every luminous body that appears in the high atmosphere is a lamp for the people of the earth. However, some of those lamps remain forever, safe from change and corruption, and some do not remain so; these are the meteors which God brings into being and makes into missiles against the devils. With this interpretation the difficulty is removed, and God knows best.

**The second question:** How is it permissible for the devils to go to a place where they know, by conjecture, that the meteors will burn them, and they will never reach their goal at all? Is it possible for such an act to proceed from a rational being? How then from the devils, who have a distinction in knowing subtle stratagems?

The answer: the occurrence of this state has no specific place, for otherwise they would not go to it. They are only prevented from reaching the places of the angels, and those places vary. Perhaps they arrive at a place where meteors strike them, and perhaps they arrive at another where they do not encounter the angels and so are not struck by meteors. When they were destroyed at some times and survived at other times, it was permissible for them to arrive at places where, in their estimation, they would probably not be struck by meteors, just as one who travels the sea may take a route in which he probably expects to be saved. This is what Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī mentioned as the answer to this question in his exegesis.

One may say: when they ascend, either they will reach the places of the angels or they will reach other than those places. If they reach the places of the angels, they will be burned; and if they reach other than the places of the angels, they will not attain their goal at all. So under both suppositions the goal is not achieved. When this experiment has taken place and it has been established by induction that attaining the goal is impossible, they must refrain from this activity and not undertake it at all. al-Qāḍī answered: The closer view is that this condition existed before the Prophet (ﷺ), but it increased in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), so that because of its abundance it became a miracle.

**[p. 107]**

**The fourth question:** The devil is created from fire, as God said, relating about Iblīs: ﴿You created me from fire﴾ [Ṣād: 76], and He said: ﴿And the jinn We had created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 27]. The answer: it is possible that although the devils are of fires, they are weak fires. If the fires of the meteors reach them, and those fires are stronger in state than they are, then the stronger necessarily nullifies the weaker. Do you not see that a weak lamp, when brought into a strong fire, is extinguished? So it is likewise here.

If what we have written here is added to what we wrote in the surah of al-Mulk and in the other verses that include this question, it reaches a complete sufficiency in this chapter. God knows best.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾ ﴿and as a protection from every rebellious devil﴾ ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side﴾ ﴿driven away, and for them is a constant punishment﴾ ﴿except one who snatches a fragment, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾.

**The first issue:** Hamzah, Hafs (on the authority of ʿAsim) recited *zīnatin* with tanwin and *al-kawākibi* in the genitive (jarr). This is the reading of Masruq ibn al-Ajdaʿ. Al-Farrāʾ said: this is the replacement of a definite noun by an indefinite one, as in His saying ﴿bi-l-nāṣiyati, nāṣiyatin﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 15-16], where an indefinite noun is returned to a definite one. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-kawākib* is an apposition (badal) for *al-zīnah*, because it is that very thing, just as you say: "I passed by Abū ʿAbd Allāh Zayd."

ʿAsim recited *al-zīnah* with tanwin and *al-kawākiba* in the accusative. Al-Farrāʾ said: he means "We adorned the stars." Al-Zajjāj said: it is permissible that *al-kawākib* in the accusative be an apposition for His saying ﴿bi-zīnatin﴾, since ﴿bi-zīnatin﴾ is in the accusative position. The rest of the readers recited *bi-zīnati al-kawākibi* in the genitive, by way of idafa (construct phrase).

The first: obtaining adornment.

The second: protection from the rebellious devil. Therefore, we must examine what is said about these three matters.

As for the first:

[p. 106 ends here — no; this is p. 105 continuing] It is the adornment of the lowest heaven with these stars. One may say: it has been established in ʿilm al-hayʾah (astronomy/cosmology) that these fixed stars are set in the eighth sphere, and that the six planets are set in the six spheres that surround the lowest heaven. The answer: people living on the surface of the sphere of the earth, when they look at the sky, see it adorned with these stars. Moreover, we have already explained in ʿilm al-hayʾah that the philosophers have not completed a proof showing that these stars are set in the eighth heaven. Perhaps we explained this matter in the commentary on the surah ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk: 1], in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

**The first discussion:** *al-zīnah* is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like *al-nisbah*, and also a noun for that with which something is adorned, as *al-līqah* is a noun for that with which the inkwell is smeared. The author of al-Kashshāf said: His saying ﴿bi-zīnati al-kawākib﴾ allows both. If you intend the verbal noun, then its idafa is to the agent, meaning that its adornment is the stars; or its idafa is to the object, meaning that God adorned the stars and beautified them, because the heaven was only adorned by their goodness in themselves. **The second discussion:** In explaining how the stars are an adornment for the heaven, there are several aspects:

The first: light and radiance are among the best and most perfect attributes. When these shining, illuminating stars are present on the surface of the heaven, the light and radiance remain in the body of the heaven because of the presence of these stars in it. The fourth aspect: when a person in a dark night looks at the surface of the heaven and sees these luminous jewels shining, sparkling and glittering on that blue surface, there is no doubt that they are the best and most perfect of things in composition and substance, and all of this shows that these stars are an adornment.

It has been said: it is the one who cannot be overpowered (lā yutamakkanu minhu), and its root is from smoothness (al-malāsah); from this comes His saying ﴿a palace of smooth glass (ṣarḥun mumarrad)﴾ [al-Naml: 44], and from it comes *al-amrad* (the beardless youth). We say: the full investigation of this is mentioned at His saying: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. It is known that this did not happen at all, for the numbers of the stars of the heaven remain in one state without any change whatsoever. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 8–10:

Regarding His words ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, recited ﴿lā yassamma'ūna﴾ with a doubled *sīn* and *mīm*. Its original form is *yatasamma'ūna*, and the *tā'* was assimilated into the *sīn* because both share the quality of *hams* (breathiness). *Tasamma'a* (to strain to hear) means seeking to hear; it is said: "He strained to hear" whether or not he heard. The rest recited it with a single, unstressed *sīn*. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the doubled form in *yassamma'ūna*. He said: "The Arabs say *tasamma'tu ilā fulān* (I strained to hear so-and-so), and they say *sami'tu fulānan* (I heard so-and-so), but they hardly ever say *sami'tu ilā fulān*." It has also been said, in support of this recitation, that when straining to hear is negated, hearing itself is negated.

The proof for the second recitation is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing﴾ (Al-Shu'ara 26:212). Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the devils would strain to listen to the exalted assembly, and then they were prevented so that they could not hear. The proponents of the first recitation may answer: the explicit statement that they are removed from hearing does not prevent them also being removed from straining to hear, as indicated by this verse. Indeed, it is even stronger in repelling the devils and preventing them from eavesdropping on news of the heavens, for whoever is prevented from straining to listen is all the more prevented from hearing.

**The second issue:** The difference between your saying *sami'tu ḥadītha fulān* (I heard so-and-so's speech) and *sami'tu ilā ḥadīthihi* (I listened to his speech) is that *sami'tu ḥadīthahu* indicates perception, while *sami'tu ilā ḥadīthihi* indicates attentive listening together with perception.

**The third issue:** Concerning His words ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾, there are two opinions:

The first, which is the well-known one, is that the sense of the sentence is "lest they hear." When the governing particle was omitted, the verb reverted to the nominative, as in His words: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ (An-Nisa 4:176), and as in His words: ﴿mountains lest they shake with you﴾ (An-Nahl 16:15). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The omission of *an* and of the *lām* is each permissible on its own. But their combination is among the abhorrent matters from which the Qur'an must be protected."

The second opinion, which the author of al-Kashshaf chose, is that it is an independent sentence, disconnected from what precedes it. It describes the state of those who steal hearing: they are unable to hear the speech of the angels and eavesdrop on it, since they are pelted with shooting stars, repelled and driven away from that aim.

**The fourth issue:** The exalted assembly (*al-mala' al-a'lā*) are the angels, because they dwell in the heavens. As for humans and jinn, they are the lower assembly, because they are the inhabitants of the earth.

Know that He, exalted is He, described those devils with three attributes:

The first: that they cannot listen.

The second: that they are pelted from every direction, repelled (*duḥūran*). On this there are discussions:

The first: We have already mentioned the meaning of *duḥūr* in Surah al-A'raf at His words: ﴿Go forth from it, reviled and expelled﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:18). Al-Mubarrad said: *al-duḥūr* is the greatest degradation and humiliation. Ibn Qutaybah said: "I repelled him, a repelling and a driving away," meaning I pushed him away and drove him off.

The second discussion: concerning the grammatical position (*intiṣāb*) of His words ﴿repelled (duḥūran)﴾, there are several possibilities:

The first: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with the sense of "they are repelled with repelling," and the verb is indicated by His words: ﴿and they are pelted﴾.

The second: the sense is "and they are pelted for repelling," then the *lām* was omitted.

The third: Mujahid said: "*duḥūran* means driven away." On this view it is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) expressed by a verbal noun, like *al-rukū'* (bowing), *al-sujūd* (prostration) and *al-ḥuḍūr* (presence).

The third discussion: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited *duḥūran* with an open *dāl*. Al-Farra' said: "It is as if he said: they are pelted, they are repelled by what is repelled (with it)." Then he said: "I do not favour the open *dāl*, because if it were established as correct, it would have the *bā'* (with), as you say: 'they are pelted with stones,' and you do not say 'they are pelted the stones.' However, it is permissible in general, as the poet said:"

*nughālī al-laḥma lil-aḍyāfi nī'an*
(We overprice the meat for the guests, raw)

That is: we overprice with the meat.

The third attribute: His words: ﴿And for them is a perpetual punishment﴾. The meaning is that they are stoned with shooting stars, and this punishment is inflicted upon them continuously. We have mentioned the explanation of *wāṣib* in Surah al-Nahl at His words: ﴿and His is the religion, perpetual﴾ (An-Nahl 16:52). They all said: it means "constant." Al-Wahidi said: whoever explains *wāṣib* as "severe" or "painful," that is a meaning but not an explanation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except one who snatches a fragment﴾. We have mentioned the meaning of *khaṭf* (snatching) in Surah al-Hajj. Al-Zajjaj said: it is taking a thing swiftly, and the origin of *khaṭifa* is *ikhtaṭafa*. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "*man* (whoever) is in the nominative position as a substitute for the *wāw* in *lā yassamma'ūna*, meaning: the devils do not eavesdrop except the devil who snatches the fragment, that is, steals the word by way of stealthy pilfering." ﴿Then he is pursued﴾ means he is overtaken and struck. It is said: *tabi'ahu* and *atba'ahu*, when one goes in his track, and *atba'ahu* when one overtakes him. Its origin is His words: ﴿Then Satan pursued him﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:175), and its explanation has already passed.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿a piercing flame (shihāb thāqib)﴾. Al-Hasan said: *thāqib* means shining. I say: it was named *thāqib* because its light pierces the air. Ibn 'Abbas, explaining His words ﴿the piercing star﴾ (At-Tariq 86:3), said: it is a man who was named thus because he pierces with his light the sky of the seven heavens. And Allah knows best.

The third discussion: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited *duḥūran* with an open *dāl*. Al-Farra' said: "It is as if he said: they are pelted, they are repelled by what is repelled (with it)." Then he said: "I do not favour the open *dāl*, because if it were established as correct, it would have the *bā'* (with), as you say: 'they are pelted with stones,' and you do not say 'they are pelted the stones.' *nughālī al-laḥma lil-aḍyāfi nī'an*
(We overprice the meat for the guests, raw)

That is: we overprice with the meat.

The third attribute: His words: ﴿And for them is a perpetual punishment﴾. The meaning is that they are stoned with shooting stars, and this punishment is inflicted upon them continuously. We have mentioned the explanation of *wāṣib* in Surah al-Nahl at His words: ﴿and His is the religion, perpetual﴾ (An-Nahl 16:52). They all said: it means "constant." Al-Wahidi said: whoever explains *wāṣib* as "severe" or "painful," that is a meaning but not an explanation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except one who snatches a fragment﴾. We have mentioned the meaning of *khaṭf* (snatching) in Surah al-Hajj. Al-Zajjaj said: it is taking a thing swiftly, and the origin of *khaṭifa* is *ikhtaṭafa*. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "*man* (whoever) is in the nominative position as a substitute for the *wāw* in *lā yassamma'ūna*, meaning: the devils do not eavesdrop except the devil who snatches the fragment, that is, steals the word by way of stealthy pilfering." ﴿Then he is pursued﴾ means he is overtaken and struck. It is said: *tabi'ahu* and *atba'ahu*, when one goes in his track, and *atba'ahu* when one overtakes him. Its origin is His words: ﴿Then Satan pursued him﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:175), and its explanation has already passed.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿a piercing flame (shihāb thāqib)﴾. Al-Hasan said: *thāqib* means shining. I say: it was named *thāqib* because its light pierces the air. Ibn 'Abbas, explaining His words ﴿the piercing star﴾ (At-Tariq 86:3), said: it is a man who was named thus because he pierces with his light the sky of the seven heavens. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 8–10:

Regarding His words ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, recited ﴿lā yassamma'ūna﴾ with a doubled *sīn* and *mīm*. Its original form is *yatasamma'ūna*, and the *tā'* was assimilated into the *sīn* because both share the quality of *hams* (breathiness). *Tasamma'a* (to strain to hear) means seeking to hear; it is said: "He strained to hear" whether or not he heard. The rest recited it with a single, unstressed *sīn*. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the doubled form in *yassamma'ūna*. He said: "The Arabs say *tasamma'tu ilā fulān* (I strained to hear so-and-so), and they say *sami'tu fulānan* (I heard so-and-so), but they hardly ever say *sami'tu ilā fulān*." It has also been said, in support of this recitation, that when straining to hear is negated, hearing itself is negated.

The proof for the second recitation is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing﴾ (Al-Shu'ara 26:212). Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the devils would strain to listen to the exalted assembly, and then they were prevented so that they could not hear. The proponents of the first recitation may answer: the explicit statement that they are removed from hearing does not prevent them also being removed from straining to hear, as indicated by this verse. Indeed, it is even stronger in repelling the devils and preventing them from eavesdropping on news of the heavens, for whoever is prevented from straining to listen is all the more prevented from hearing.

**The second issue:** The difference between your saying *sami'tu ḥadītha fulān* (I heard so-and-so's speech) and *sami'tu ilā ḥadīthihi* (I listened to his speech) is that *sami'tu ḥadīthahu* indicates perception, while *sami'tu ilā ḥadīthihi* indicates attentive listening together with perception.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verse 11:

[p. 109] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask them: Are they the more difficult to create, or those We have created? Indeed We created them from clinging clay.﴾ In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: on the arrangement (nazm) of the verse. Know that we have mentioned that the ultimate purpose of this noble Book is to establish the four foundations: the divine (al-ilahiyyat), the return (al-ma'ad), prophethood (al-nubuwwah), and the establishment of qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination). We say: He, exalted is He, opened this surah by establishing what indicates the existence of the Creator and indicates His oneness, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and the creation of the easts and the wests. Then, when He had firmly established discourse on this matter, He built upon it the affirmation of the doctrine of resurrection, gathering and rising (al-hashr wa'l-nashr), and the Day of Resurrection (al-qiyamah).

Know that discussion of this issue relates to two aspects:

The first of them: establishing rational possibility (al-jawaz al-'aqli).

The second of them: establishing actual occurrence (al-wuqu').

As for the discussion of the first aim: know that proof of a thing occurs in two ways:

One of them: that it is said that He has power over what is harder, more difficult and more arduous than it, so it is necessary that He also has power over it.

The second: that it is said: He has power over it in one of two states, while the agent and the receptive subject remain as they were, so it is necessary that the power over it remain in the second state. God, exalted is He, mentioned these two methods in explaining that the doctrine of resurrection and the Day of Resurrection is a matter that is permissible and possible.

As for the first method, it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So ask them: Are they the more difficult to create?﴾ [al-Saffat: 11]. The meaning is as if He, exalted is He, were saying: Ask them, O Muhammad, these deniers: are they harder to create than the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and the creation of the easts and the wests, and the creation of the devils who ascend to the heavens? There is no doubt that they acknowledge that the creation of this category is more arduous and more difficult in common usage than the creation of the first category. So when it has been established by the proofs mentioned in establishing divine oneness that He, exalted is He, has power over this category which is harder and more difficult, then it is more fitting that He has power over restoring life to these bodies. A parallel to this inference is His saying, exalted is He, at the end of Ya Sin: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 81], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57].

As for the second method, it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed We created them from clinging clay.﴾ The meaning is that these bodies are receptive to life, for if they were not receptive to life they would not have become living the first time. And God is able to create this life in these bodies; had He not been able to do this, life would not have come about the first time. There is no doubt that the receptivity of those bodies remains, and that God's power remains, because this receptivity and this power are among the essential attributes (al-sifat al-dhatiyyah), so their cessation is impossible. Thus by these two methods it is established that the doctrine of resurrection and the Day of Resurrection is possible. When He, exalted is He, had clarified the possibility of this meaning by these two methods, He clarified its occurrence by His saying: ﴿Say: Yes, and you will be abased﴾ [al-Saffat: 18]. This is because the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ has been established on account of the manifestation of miracles through him, and whoever is truthful, when he reports a matter whose occurrence is possible, it is obligatory to acknowledge its occurrence. This is the explanation of the arrangement of this verse, and it is in the utmost beauty; and God knows best.

The second issue: on the interpretation of the words of this verse. As for His saying: ﴿So ask them﴾, it means that since it has been established by decisive proofs that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, then ask these deniers, and say to them: ﴿Are they the more difficult to create﴾, or these things whose being created by Him we have explained? He did not relate of them that they admitted that the creation of these things is more arduous, because this is evident as something known by necessity, so there is no need to report from them the correctness of the matter being so.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed We created them from clinging clay﴾, meaning: since We were able to create life in their essences first, it is obligatory that We remain able to create life in them a second time; because we have explained that the state of the receptive subject and the state of the agent cannot change.

There is another subtle point in this: the people said: How is it conceivable that a human being should be generated neither from a drop of semen nor from two parents? It is as if it were said to them: Since you have acknowledged the origination of the world, and have admitted that the heavens and the earth and what is between them came into being only through God's creating and bringing into existence, then you must admit that the first human being came into being without parents. When you have understood that and acknowledged it, then your saying "how does a human come into being without semen and without parents?" has collapsed. Also, it is well known among the majority that Adam was created from clinging clay, and whoever is able to create life in clinging clay, how could He be incapable of restoring life to these essences?

As for the manner of the creation of man from clinging clay, it is mentioned in the preceding surah. Know that this interpretation is appropriate only if we say that what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We created them from clinging clay﴾ is that We created their father Adam from clinging clay. There are other interpretations, namely that what is meant is that We created every human being from clinging clay. Its explanation: animal life is generated only from semen and menstrual blood, and semen is generated from blood; so animal life is generated only from blood, and blood is generated only from nourishment, and nourishment is either animal or vegetable. As for the generation of the animal that has become food, the discussion of how it is generated is like the discussion of the generation of man. So it is established that the basis of foods is plants, and plants are generated only from the mixing of earth with water, which is clinging clay. If that is so, then it has become clear that all creation is generated from clinging clay. Having established this, we say: these parts from which this clinging clay is composed are receptive to life, and God, exalted is He, is able over them; and this receptivity and this ability are necessarily enduring, so it is necessary that this validity remain at all times. These are clear and evident explanations. As for "lazib" (lazib, clinging), it is said to mean adhering, and it is said to mean sticky, and it is said: the clay of the riverbank. Most lexicographers hold that the ba' in lazib is a substitute for the mim, it being said: lazib and lazim.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, you marvel, and they mock.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The argument may be formulated as follows. These deniers have acknowledged that God, exalted is He, is capable of creating things more difficult than restoring life to these bodies. It is established in clear reasons that whoever is capable of the harder and more arduous is capable of the easier and simpler. Yet despite the presence of this self-evident proof, these people have remained persistent in denying resurrection and the Last Day. This is a matter of intense wonder: how can it be conceived that these people remain persistent in this when such a clear and manifest proof has appeared? So you, O Muhammad, marvel at their persistence in denial, while they have reached the extreme of denial to the point that they mock you for your statement affirming the gathering, the raising, the resurrection, and the Last Day. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Rather, you marvel, and they mock.﴾

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ʿajibtu (عَجِبْتُ) with a damma on the tා (the first person form, "I marvel"), while the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Wahidi said: The damma is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Ibrahim, Yahya ibn Thabit, al-Aʿmash, the reading of the people of Kufa, and the choice of Abu ʿUbayda. As for those who read with a fatha, they argued with several points:

First: The reading with a damma indicates attributing wonder to God, exalted is He, and that is impossible, because wonder is a state that arises from ignorance of the nature of a thing, and it is known that ignorance is impossible for God.

Second: God, exalted is He, attributed wonder to Muhammad ﷺ in another verse on this same matter, when He said: ﴿And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying, "When we have become dust?"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5].

Third: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, you marvel, and they mock.﴾ Apparently they mocked because of that wonder, so when they mocked him, that wonder must have proceeded from him.

As for those who read with a damma on the tā', they answered the first argument in several ways:

First: We do not concede that the reading with a damma indicates attributing wonder to God, exalted is He. Its explanation is that the sense would be: "Say, O Muhammad, (Rather, I marvel, and they mock)." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Hear them and see them﴾ [Maryam: 38], meaning: "How well they hear and see what you say about them," and likewise His saying: ﴿How patient they are over the Fire!﴾ [al-Baqarah: 175].

Second: Even granting that this entails attributing wonder to God, exalted is He, why do you say that is impossible? It is related that Shurayh used to prefer the reading with a fatha and would say: "Wonder befits only one who does not know." Al-A'mash said: I mentioned that to Ibrahim, and he said: "Shurayh was impressed by his own knowledge, whereas ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) was more knowledgeable, and he would read with a damma."

The verification of the matter is that we say: The Qur'an and the report both indicate the permissibility of attributing wonder to God, exalted is He. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying﴾ [al-Ra'd: 5]; meaning: "And if you marvel, O Muhammad, at their saying, it is also a marvel in My sight." It has been answered that it is not impossible that the intended meaning is: "And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying in your estimation." As for the report, it is His ﷺ saying: "Your Lord marvels at your despair and your recent despairing, and your Lord marvels at a young man who has no inclination toward youthful folly." 

Once this is established, we say: wonder from God, exalted is He, differs from wonder from human beings, just as He said: ﴿And they plot, and God plots﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], and He said: ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 79], and He said: ﴿And He is their deceiver﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]. Plotting, deceiving, and mocking from God, exalted is He, are different from these states when they come from servants. We have already mentioned that the rule in this matter is that such expressions are to be understood in terms of the ultimate outcomes of the attributes, not their initial manifestations.

Likewise here: whoever marvels at something considers it great. So wonder with respect to God, exalted is He, is to be understood as God considering that state great: if it is ugly, a great punishment follows from it, and if it is good, a great reward follows from it. This is the complete discussion of this debate. The closest view is that one should say: if the reading with a damma is established by mass transmission (tawatur), it is obligatory to adopt it, and its interpretation is what we have mentioned; but if this reading is not established by mass transmission, then the reading with a fatha on the tā' is preferable. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 17–20:**

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ ﴿And they say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ ﴿"And our forefathers of old?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Yes, and you will be humbled."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had established the decisive proof for the possibility of resurrection and the Day of Judgment, He related several things about the deniers:

The first of them: the Prophet (ﷺ) is astonished at their persistence in denial while they mock him for his persistence in affirmation. This indicates that he (ﷺ) and those peoples were at the extreme of distance from one another and at opposite ends of the spectrum.

The second is His saying: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾

The third is His saying: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ It must be that what is meant by this second and third is other than the first, because conjunction (ʿaṭf) requires difference, and repetition is contrary to the original principle. What I hold in this matter is that it may be said: the people were finding the gathering and the Day of Judgment far-fetched, and they would say: "How can someone who has died, become dust, and whose parts have been scattered throughout the world, be conceived of returning as the same self?" They went so far in this far-fetchedness that they would mock whoever held this view. Given that this is so, there is no way to remove this far-fetchedness from them except by two means:

One of them: that He presents to them the proof that indicates the soundness of the gathering and the resurrection, such as saying to them: "Do you know that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater and harder than the restoration of a human being after his death? And do you know that the One who is able to do the harder and more difficult must be able to do the easier and simpler?" This proof, although clear and strong, when these premises are presented to the minds of those deniers, they do not comprehend them or stop at them; and when they are reminded, they do not recall them, because of the extreme dullness and ignorance. Therefore, they did not benefit from this kind of explanation.

The second means: that the Messenger (ﷺ) establish the fact of his mission through miracles, and then say: "Since it has been established by the miracle that my being a truthful messenger from God is true, I inform you that the resurrection and the Day of Judgment are true." Then those deniers do not benefit from this means either, because when they see an overpowering miracle and a dazzling sign, they attribute it to being magic, and they mock it and ridicule it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ Thus it has become clear through the explanation we have mentioned that these three expressions alert to these evident benefits.

Know that most people have not stopped at these subtleties, so they said: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, you wonder, and they mock.﴾

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ So it is necessary that what is meant by His saying: ﴿yastaskhirūn﴾ (they mock/ask one another to mock) be other than what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿wa-yaskharūn﴾ (and they mock). This speaker said: what is meant by His saying ﴿wa-yaskharūn﴾ is their proceeding to mockery, and what is meant by His saying ﴿yastaskhirūn﴾ is that each of them asks his companion to proceed to mockery. This obligation fell upon them only because they did not stop at the benefits we have mentioned. And God knows best.

The fourth of the matters that God, exalted is He, related about them is that they said: ﴿This is nothing but obvious magic.﴾ That is, when they see a sign and a miracle they mock it, and the cause of that mockery is their belief that it is of the category of magic. His saying ﴿mubīn﴾ (obvious) means that its being magic is a matter clear, with no doubt for anyone about it. Then God, exalted is He, explained that the cause that moves them to ridicule the claim of resurrection, to disregard the proofs indicating the soundness of that claim, and to ridicule all the miracles, is their saying: that the one who has died and whose parts have been scattered throughout the whole world, what is earthly in him has mixed with the dust of the earth, and what is watery and airy in him has mixed with the vapors of the world; so how can this human being be conceived of returning as the same self, living and understanding? This statement is what moves them to those three states mentioned earlier. Then, when God, exalted is He, related this doubt of theirs, He said: Say, O Muhammad, "Yes, and you will be humbled." God was content with this measure of answer only because He had mentioned in the previous verse, by decisive and certain demonstration, that it is a possible matter. When the necessary possibility is established, there is no way to be certain of its occurrence except by the report of a truthful informant. Since the miracles stand as evidence for the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), his word is binding as truth, and so his mere saying ﴿Say, "Yes"﴾ becomes a decisive proof of its occurrence.

Whoever reflects on these verses will know that they came in the best arrangement, because He demonstrated the possibility by rational proof and demonstrated the occurrence of that possible matter by transmitted proof. It is well known that adding anything beyond this explanation would be like an impossible matter.

As for His saying ﴿awa-ābāʾunā﴾ (or our forefathers): the meaning is "Will our forefathers too be resurrected?" This interrogative alif (the hamza of interrogation) entered upon the conjunctive particle. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir recited it here, and in Surat al-Wāqiʿa with the waw silent. We have discussed this matter in Surat al-Aʿrāf at His saying: ﴿awa-amina ahl al-qurā﴾ (Or did the people of the cities feel secure?) [al-Aʿrāf: 98].

As for His saying ﴿Qul naʿam﴾ (Say, "Yes"), we say: al-Kisāʾī alone recited ﴿naʿim﴾ with a kasra on the ʿayn.

As for His saying ﴿wa-antum dākhirūn﴾ (and you will be humbled), that is, ṣāghirūn (abased). Abū ʿUbayd said: al-dukhūr is the most intense abasement. We have explained this word at His saying: ﴿sujjadan lillāh wa-hum dākhirūn﴾ (prostrating to God while they are humbled) [al-Naḥl: 48].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 17–20:**

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ ﴿And they say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ ﴿"And our forefathers of old?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Yes, and you will be humbled."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had established the decisive proof for the possibility of resurrection and the Day of Judgment, He related several things about the deniers:

The first of them: the Prophet (ﷺ) is astonished at their persistence in denial while they mock him for his persistence in affirmation. This indicates that he (ﷺ) and those peoples were at the extreme of distance from one another and at opposite ends of the spectrum.

The second is His saying: ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾

The third is His saying: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ It must be that what is meant by this second and third is other than the first, because conjunction (ʿaṭf) requires difference, and repetition is contrary to the original principle. What I hold in this matter is that it may be said: the people were finding the gathering and the Day of Judgment far-fetched, and they would say: "How can someone who has died, become dust, and whose parts have been scattered throughout the world, be conceived of returning as the same self?" They went so far in this far-fetchedness that they would mock whoever held this view. Given that this is so, there is no way to remove this far-fetchedness from them except by two means:

One of them: that He presents to them the proof that indicates the soundness of the gathering and the resurrection, such as saying to them: "Do you know that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater and harder than the restoration of a human being after his death? Therefore, they did not benefit from this kind of explanation.

This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ Thus it has become clear through the explanation we have mentioned that these three expressions alert to these evident benefits.

Know that most people have not stopped at these subtleties, so they said: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, you wonder, and they mock.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 21–24:

The Exalted said: ﴿It will be but a single cry, and at once they will be looking on.﴾ ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ ﴿"This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny."﴾

Know that when the Exalted, in the preceding verse, explained what proves the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day, and then followed it with what proves the occurrence of the Last Day, He mentioned in these verses some details of the circumstances of the Last Day. He, the Exalted, mentioned in this verse several types of those circumstances.

The first circumstance is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It will be but a single cry, and at once they will be looking on.﴾ Concerning it there are several discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿fa-innama﴾ ("it will be but") is the answer to an implied conditional clause, and the meaning is: "If it is so, then it is but a single cry."

The second discussion: The pronoun in His saying ﴿innama hiya﴾ ("it is but") is a pronoun referring to what is explained by what follows. The meaning is: "The resurrection is but a single cry."

The third discussion: Al-zajrah (the cry) in the lexicon is the shout by which one drives (yuzjaru bi-ha), like the driving of cattle and camels when they are being driven. Its use then became frequent until it came to mean "the shout," even where there is no sense of driving, as in this verse. I say: It is not far-fetched to say that this shout was called a zajrah because it drives the dead away from lying in their graves and urges them to rise from the graves and to present themselves at the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. Having understood this, we say: What is meant by this zajrah is what the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. By the first blast they die, and by the second blast they come to life and stand up. Here there are questions:

The first question: What is the benefit of this shout, since the people at that time are dead? For the blast functions as the cause of their life, so it precedes the occurrence of their life. It thus follows that this shout occurs while creation is dead, and so that shout would be without benefit; it would be pointless, and pointlessness is not permissible in the acts of God.

The answer: As for our companions, they say that God does what He wills. As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), al-Qadi said: In this there are two aspects:

The first: that the angels take a lesson from it.

The second: that the benefit is intimidation and terror.

The second question: Does that shout have any effect in restoring life?

The answer: No, as evidence that the first shout brought about death and the second brought about life. That indicates that the shout has no effect either in death or in life. Rather, the Creator of death and life is God, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

The third question: Is that shout the voice of the angels, or does God create it directly?

The answer: All of this is permissible. However, it has been related that God, the Exalted, commands Israfil (Isrāfīl) to call out: "O decayed bones, O worn-out skins, O scattered parts, gather together by the permission of God, the Exalted."

Page 114

The fourth term among the terms mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and behold, they will be looking on﴾. It may mean that they look at what is happening to them, and it may mean that some of them look at others, and it may mean: they look at the resurrection which they denied.

The second circumstance from the events of the Last Day is what God reported about them: that after rising from the graves they said: ﴿"Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Woe" (al-wayl) is a word that the speaker says at the time of destruction. The intended meaning is that when they witnessed the resurrection, they said: ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment"﴾, that is, "This is the Day of Recompense." The point is that the Exalted mentioned in many verses of the Qur'an that we see in this world the righteous and the wicked, the disobedient and the sincere, the heretic and the believer, and we see that what befits them of recompense does not reach them in this world. Therefore it is necessary to affirm the Last Day: ﴿so that He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. In sum, this shows that recompense occurs only after death. The unbelievers, though they heard this strong evidence, denied it and rebelled. Then, when the Exalted revives them on the Day of Resurrection and they witness the resurrection, they remember that day and say: ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment"﴾, that is, the Day of Recompense about which God gave many proofs in the Qur'an, but "we denied them." A parallel is that one who was warned of something and paid no attention to it, then saw it afterward, may say, "This is the day of such-and-such event." So it is here. There is another possibility: the Exalted said in the opening surah: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4], thereby clarifying that there is no master on that day except God. So their saying "This is the Day of Judgment" is an indication that this is the day on which no one has any judgment except God. They mentioned it only because of the intense fear that had entered their hearts.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿"This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny."﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first: They differed as to whether this is part of the speech of the unbelievers, or whether their speech ended at His saying: ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ As for His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Decision"﴾, it is the speech of others. Some of them held the first view and claimed that His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Decision"﴾ and the verse that follows is part of what some of them said to others. Most scholars hold the second view, and they argued with two points:

The first: His saying ﴿"which you used to deny"﴾ is addressed by some of them to others, and it is a direct address to all the unbelievers; therefore the speaker of these words must be someone other than the unbelievers.

The second: His saying ﴿"Gather those who did wrong and their spouses"﴾ [al-Saffat: 22] follows on from His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny."﴾ Since His saying ﴿"Gather those who did wrong"﴾ is the speech of someone other than the unbelievers, likewise His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny"﴾ must be the speech of someone other than the unbelievers. On this view, His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment"﴾ is the speech of the unbelievers, and His saying ﴿"This is the Day of Decision"﴾ is the speech of the angels, answering them. The reason it is an answer to them is that those unbelievers believed of themselves that they were right in rejecting the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, and that they were right in those corrupt religions. So they said: ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment"﴾, that is, this is the day on which the reward of our obedience and our good deeds reaches us. So the angels say to them: On this day, appearances carry no weight, for on this day the true reward is distinguished from the apparent reward, and true acts of obedience are separated from acts of obedience tainted by show and reputation. In this way, this speech from the angels became an answer to what the unbelievers had said.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 37, verses 21–24:

The Exalted said: ﴿It will be but a single cry, and at once they will be looking on.﴾ ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ ﴿"This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny."﴾

Know that when the Exalted, in the preceding verse, explained what proves the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day, and then followed it with what proves the occurrence of the Last Day, He mentioned in these verses some details of the circumstances of the Last Day. He, the Exalted, mentioned in this verse several types of those circumstances.

The first circumstance is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It will be but a single cry, and at once they will be looking on.﴾ Concerning it there are several discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿fa-innama﴾ ("it will be but") is the answer to an implied conditional clause, and the meaning is: "If it is so, then it is but a single cry."

The second discussion: The pronoun in His saying ﴿innama hiya﴾ ("it is but") is a pronoun referring to what is explained by what follows. The meaning is: "The resurrection is but a single cry."

The third discussion: Al-zajrah (the cry) in the lexicon is the shout by which one drives (yuzjaru bi-ha), like the driving of cattle and camels when they are being driven. Its use then became frequent until it came to mean "the shout," even where there is no sense of driving, as in this verse. I say: It is not far-fetched to say that this shout was called a zajrah because it drives the dead away from lying in their graves and urges them to rise from the graves and to present themselves at the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. Having understood this, we say: What is meant by this zajrah is what the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. By the first blast they die, and by the second blast they come to life and stand up. Here there are questions:

The first question: What is the benefit of this shout, since the people at that time are dead? For the blast functions as the cause of their life, so it precedes the occurrence of their life. It thus follows that this shout occurs while creation is dead, and so that shout would be without benefit; it would be pointless, and pointlessness is not permissible in the acts of God.

The answer: As for our companions, they say that God does what He wills. As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), al-Qadi said: In this there are two aspects:

The first: that the angels take a lesson from it.

The second: that the benefit is intimidation and terror.

The second question: Does that shout have any effect in restoring life?

The answer: No, as evidence that the first shout brought about death and the second brought about life. That indicates that the shout has no effect either in death or in life. Rather, the Creator of death and life is God, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

The third question: Is that shout the voice of the angels, or does God create it directly?

The answer: All of this is permissible. However, it has been related that God, the Exalted, commands Israfil (Isrāfīl) to call out: "O decayed bones, O worn-out skins, O scattered parts, gather together by the permission of God, the Exalted."
