Then Allah, exalted is He, compels the people of the Fire to partake of some of its parts.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ there are several views:

The first: it became a trial for the wrongdoers in that when the disbelievers heard this verse, they said: "How is it conceivable that a tree should grow in Hell, when the Fire burns trees?"

The answer to this is that the Creator of the Fire is able to prevent the Fire from burning the tree. Moreover, if it is permissible that there be guardians (zabaniyah) in the Fire while Allah prevents the Fire from burning them, why should the like not be permissible for this tree? Once you know this question, and the answer, the meaning of the zaqqum tree being a trial for the wrongdoers is that when they heard this verse, that doubt entered their hearts, and that doubt became a cause for their persistence in disbelief. This is what is meant by it being a trial for them.

The second interpretation is that the intended meaning is that this tree becomes a trial for them in the Fire; for when they are obligated to partake of it and it is hard for them, then it becomes a trial for them.

The third interpretation: that the intended meaning of trial (fitnah) is testing and examination, for this is a matter far removed from custom and habit, contrary to what is familiar and known. So when it reaches the hearing of a believer, he entrusts its knowledge to Allah; and when it reaches a heretic (zindiq), he uses it as a means to attack the Qur'an and prophethood.

Page 124

Then, when He mentioned this tree, He described it with attributes:

The first attribute: His saying, "Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hell-fire." It was said: its place of growth is at the bottom of Hell, and its branches rise up to its levels.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿Its fruit-spathes are as if they were the heads of devils.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: talʿ (spathe/fruit-bud) is for the palm tree, so it was borrowed for what emerges from the zaqqum tree as its bearing, either as a lexical metaphor or a semantic metaphor. Ibn Qutaybah said: it was called "ṭalʿ" because it emerges (ṭulūʿ) every year, and for this reason it is said: "ṭalʿ al-nakhl" for the first thing that comes out of its fruit. As for the comparison of this ṭalʿ to the heads of devils, there is a question in it: it is said: "We have not seen the heads of devils, so how can anything be compared to them?" They answered this in several ways:

The first, which is the correct one: when people believed that angels possess perfect excellence in form and conduct, they believed that devils possess the utmost ugliness and deformity in form and conduct. Just as comparison to an angel is fine when intending to establish perfection and excellence, as in His saying: ﴿This is nothing but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31], so likewise it is fitting that comparison to the heads of devils be fine for ugliness and deformity of creation. The upshot is that this is a comparison not to the perceptible but to the imagined: as if it were said that the most hideous things in imagination and conception are the heads of devils, and this tree resembles them in the ugliness of its appearance and the deformity of its form. What confirms this is that when intelligent people see something highly disturbing, unusual in form, and hideous in creation, they say: "It is a devil"; and when they see something beautiful in form and conduct, they say: "It is an angel." Imru' al-Qays said:

"Will you kill me while the sharp sword is my bedfellow, and notched blades, blue, like the fangs of ghouls?"

The second view: the devils are snakes that have heads and crests, and they are among the most hideous of snakes, and by them the proverb of ugliness is struck. When the Arabs see an ugly sight they say: "It is like the devil of al-Hamataḥ," and al-Hamatah is a specific tree.

The third view: the heads of devils are a well-known plant with an ugly head. The first interpretation is the true answer.

Know that when He mentioned this tree and described its attributes, He made clear that the disbelievers are ﴿indeed eaters of it, and filling their bellies from it.﴾ Know that their undertaking of this eating has two possible aspects:

The first: they ate from it because of intense hunger. If it is said: "How do they eat it when it is extremely harsh, foul, and bitter in taste?" we say: one who falls into great harm may find relief in something that approximates that harm; so when Allah makes them feel intense hunger, they flee, to relieve that hunger, to partaking of this thing, even though it is of the quality you have mentioned.

The second aspect: it may be said that the zabaniyah compel them to eat from that tree, as a completion of their punishment.

Know that when they are satiated, their thirst then intensifies and they need drink. At this point Allah described their drink, saying: ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: al-shawb is a general name for anything mixed with something else, and al-hamim is hot water extremely intense in heat. The meaning is that when that intense thirst overcomes them, they are given to drink from that hamim, and then the zaqqum is mixed with the hamim—we seek refuge in Allah from both.

Know that Allah described their drink in the Qur'an with various things: among them that it is ghassaq; among them His saying: ﴿And they are given boiling water, so it cuts their intestines﴾ [Muhammad: 15]; and among them what He mentioned in this verse. If it is asked: what is the benefit of the particle "thumma" (then) in His saying: ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water﴾? We say: it has two aspects:

The first: they fill their bellies with the tree of al-Zaqqum, which is hot and burns

Page 125

their bellies, so their thirst increases; then they are not given to drink except after a long period. The purpose is to complete the punishment.

The second: He mentioned the food with that foulness and repugnance, then described the drink with what is more repugnant than it; so the purpose of "thumma" is to show that the condition of the drink in repugnance is greater than the condition of the food. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hell-fire.﴾ Muqatil said: that is, after eating the zaqqum and drinking the hamim. This indicates that when they were drinking the hamim they were not in Hell, and that is because the hamim comes from a place outside Hell; they are brought to the hamim for drinking as camels are brought to water, and then they are brought back to Hell. This is Muqatil's view, and he argued for its soundness by His saying: ﴿This is Hell which the criminals used to deny. They will circulate between it and scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Rahman: 43–44], and this indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned. Then, when He described their punishment in their eating and drinking, He said: ﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray.﴾ ﴿So they were hastening in their footsteps.﴾ Al-Farra' said: al-ihrā' is hastening; it is said: hara'a and ahra'a when one is urged on. The meaning is that they follow their fathers in haste, as if they were being driven to follow their fathers. The purpose of the verse is that He, exalted is He, gave as the reason for their deserving to fall into all those hardships the imitation of fathers in religion and the abandonment of following evidence; and had there been no verse in the Qur'an other than this one condemning blind imitation, it would have sufficed.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned to His Messenger what would console him regarding their disbelief and denial, saying: ﴿And certainly did most of the earlier people go astray before them.﴾ ﴿And certainly We sent among them warners.﴾ Thus He, exalted is He, made clear that His sending of messengers had already preceded and that their denial had already passed; and it must be that he ﷺ has an example in them, so that he may be patient as they were patient, and persist in calling to Allah even if they rebel; for upon him there is only the delivering (of the message).

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned?﴾ Although this is outwardly an address to the Messenger ﷺ, its real purpose is an address to the disbelievers; for they have heard the reports of all the kinds of punishment that befell the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others. If they did not know that, then there is at least a suspicion and fear fit to be a deterrent for them from their disbelief.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾, there are two views:

One of them: it is an exception from His saying: ﴿And certainly did most of the earlier people go astray before them.﴾

The second: it is an exception from His saying: ﴿How was the end of those who were warned?﴾ for their end was the worst and most horrible of ends, except the end of the sincere servants of Allah, for it was accompanied by good and ease.

**The First Story: the story of Noah (peace be upon him)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Noah certainly called upon Us, and We are the best of those who respond﴾ ﴿and We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾ ﴿and We made his descendants the surviving ones﴾ ﴿and We left for him among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾.

[p. 126]

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had said earlier: ﴿And most of the former peoples had indeed strayed before them﴾, and said: ﴿So see what was the end of those who were warned﴾, He followed this with an account of the events concerning the prophets, peace be upon them.

The first story is an account of Noah's condition, peace be upon him. About His saying: ﴿And Noah certainly called upon Us, and We are the best of those who respond﴾, there are several discussions:

The first: the lām (لَام, the emphatic lām) in His saying ﴿fa-la-ni'ma al-mujībūn﴾ (فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ) is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam), and the subject of praise (al-makhṣūṣ bil-madḥ) is omitted; that is, "We are indeed the best of those who respond."

The second discussion: He, the Exalted, mentioned that Noah called upon Him, but He did not mention in which of the events that calling took place. Therefore two views arose:

The first, which is the well-known view of the majority: he called upon the Lord, the Exalted, to save him from the trial of drowning and the distress of that event.

The second view: when Noah, peace be upon him, was occupied with calling his people to the true religion, they went to great lengths in harming him and intended to kill him. Then he, peace be upon him, called upon his Lord and sought His help against the disbelievers of his people. Allah, the Exalted, answered him and prevented them from killing and harming him. The proponent of this view argued against the weakness of the first view by saying: he, peace be upon him, only prayed against them so that Allah, the Exalted, would save him and his family, and Allah answered his supplication concerning it. So that deliverance was like something known and certain within his supplication, and this prevents saying that the goal of this calling was the attainment of that deliverance.

Then, when He, the Exalted, related about Noah that he called upon Him, He said after it: ﴿fa-la-ni'ma al-mujībūn﴾ (فَلَنِعْمَ المُجِيبُونَ), and this expression indicates that this response was among great blessings. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: He, the Exalted, expressed His Self in the plural form, saying: ﴿And Noah certainly called upon Us﴾. The Mighty Capable One is fitting only for great kindness.

The second: He repeated the plural form in His saying: ﴿fa-la-ni'ma al-mujībūn﴾, and this also indicates the magnification of that blessing, especially since He described that response as a blessed response (ni'mat al-ijābah).

The third: the fā' (فَ, "then/so") in His saying ﴿fa-la-ni'ma al-mujībūn﴾ indicates that the occurrence of this response is consequent upon that calling. A ruling that is consequent upon a fitting attribute requires that it be caused by it. This indicates that calling upon Him with sincerity is a cause for the occurrence of the response. Then, when He, the Exalted, clarified in general terms that He is the best of responders, He clarified that the bounty was granted in that response in several aspects:

The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾. According to the first view, this distress is the anguish caused by fear of drowning; according to the second, it is the distress caused by the harm of his people.

The second: His saying: ﴿And We made his descendants the surviving ones﴾, which conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), and this indicates that everyone other than him and his descendants has perished. Ibn ʿAbbās said: his descendants are his three sons: Sām (Sam), Ḥām (Ham), and Yāfith (Japheth). Sam is the father of the Arabs, the Persians, and the Romans; Ham is the father of the Sudanese; and Yafith is the father of the Turks.

The third blessing: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾, meaning that they mention this phrase. If it is said: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿among the worlds﴾? We say: its meaning is the supplication for this greeting to be established among all of them, that is, none of them is free from it. It is as if it were said: Allah established peace upon Noah and perpetuated it among the angels and the two species (humans and jinn), so that they all greet him wholeheartedly. Then, when He, the Exalted, explained the details of His favor upon him, He said: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾. The meaning is: We singled out Noah, peace be upon him, with those lofty honors, by making the world filled with his descendants and by preserving his good remembrance on the tongues of all the worlds,

[p. 127]

because he was a doer of good. Then He gave the reason for his being a doer of good: that he was a servant of Allah and a believer. The purpose of this is to show that the greatest of ranks and the most noble of stations is faith in Allah and submission to His obedience.

The second story: the story of Abraham, peace be upon him.

﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham.﴾ ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ ﴿Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?﴾ ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ ﴿Then he glanced at the stars.﴾ ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating.﴾ ﴿Then he slipped away to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand.﴾ ﴿Then they came toward him, hastening.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first: Studying the knowledge of the stars is not permissible, so how did Abraham undertake it?

The first: He glanced a glance at the stars at times of night and day, and a sickness such as fever would come upon him at certain hours of night and day, so he looked to know whether it was at that hour, and said: "Indeed, I am ill," making it an excuse for staying behind from the festival they had. The second: The scholars of usul (legal theory) said: The intended meaning is that he lived and died upon the purity of the heart from every defilement of sins, so it includes his being free from shirk, from doubt, from rancor, deceit, spite and envy.

From Ibn Abbas: he used to love for people what he loved for himself, and all people were safe from his deceit and his injustice; and Allah made him submit, so He did not equate anyone with Him. Those who held the first opinion argued that after this phrase He mentioned his denunciation of his people's shirk with Allah, which is His saying: "When he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'" Those who held the second opinion argued that the wording is absolute, so it is not restricted by one attribute rather than another, and this is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already given Abraham his right guidance before, and We were knowing of him.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 51]. Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and He said: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain [in faith].﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. If it is asked: what is the meaning of "coming to his Lord with his heart"? We say: its meaning is that he sincerely dedicated his heart to Allah, so it is as if he presented that heart as a gift to the presence of Allah. I have seen in the Torah that Allah said to Moses: "Answer your God with all your heart."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that Abraham came to his Lord with a sound heart, He mentioned that among the effects of that soundness was that he called his father and his people to monotheism, saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ The purpose of this speech is to disparage that way and to condemn it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ifkan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), its implied form being: "Do you desire gods other than Him as a falsehood?" He placed the object before the verb for emphasis, and placed the object of purpose before the direct object, because it was more important to him that he establish before them that they were in falsehood and vanity in their polytheism. It is also permissible that "ifkan" is a direct object, meaning: "Do you desire a falsehood?" Then he explained the falsehood by His saying: "gods other than Allah," as being falsehood in themselves. It is also permissible that it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Do you desire gods other than Allah as liars?"

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ On this there are two views:
One: Do you think of the Lord of the worlds that it is permissible to make these inanimate things partners to Him in worship?

Second: Do you think of the Lord of the worlds that He is of the same kind as these bodies, such that you made them equal to Him in worship? Thereby He alerted them that "there is nothing like unto Him."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then he glanced at the stars.﴾ ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ From Ibn Abbas: they used to engage in the knowledge of the stars, so he dealt with them according to their customary practice. The reason is that he intended to outwit them regarding their idols, to compel them to the proof that they are not worthy of worship. The next day was a festival day for them when they would go out, so he wished to stay behind from them, to remain alone in the house of the idols, so that he could break them. Here there are two questions:

The first: Studying the knowledge of the stars is not permissible, so how did Abraham undertake it?

The second: He, peace be upon him, was not ill, so when he said "Indeed, I am ill," was that a lie? Know that the scholars mentioned many answers to these two:

The first: He glanced a glance at the stars at times of night and day, and a sickness such as fever would come upon him at certain hours of night and day, so he looked to know whether it was at that hour, and said: "Indeed, I am ill," making it an excuse for staying behind from the festival they had. He was truthful in what he said, because the sickness used to come upon him at that time, and he stayed behind only for the sake of breaking their idols.

The second answer: The people of Abraham, peace be upon him, were masters of the stars; they glorified them and judged by them concerning unseen matters. Therefore Abraham looked at the stars, that is, into the sciences of the stars and their meanings, not that he looked at them with his own eyes. It is like saying: "So-and-so looked into jurisprudence and grammar." He only wanted to make them think that he knew what they knew and understood from the same sources they understood, so that when he said "Indeed, I am ill," they would rest content with his words.

As for His saying "Indeed, I am ill," its meaning is: "I will become ill," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die﴾ [az-Zumar: 30], that is, you will die.

The third answer: His saying "Then he glanced at the stars" refers to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star﴾ [al-An'am: 76], and so on through the verses. That glance was in order to learn the states of these stars, whether they are eternal or originated. And his saying "Indeed, I am ill" means: sick of heart, not knowing my Lord. And that was before puberty.

The fourth answer: Ibn Zayd said: He had a particular star, and whenever it rose in a particular configuration, Abraham would fall ill. By this induction, when he saw it rising in that particular configuration at that time, he said: "Indeed, I am ill," meaning: this sickness is certainly going to occur.

The fifth answer: His saying "Indeed, I am ill" means: sick of heart, because of that great multitude's unanimity upon disbelief and polytheism. Allah, exalted is He, said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 3].

The sixth answer: We do not concede that studying the knowledge of the stars and reasoning by comparing them is forbidden, because whoever believes that Allah, exalted is He, has specified each of these stars with a power and a property for which a particular effect appears from it, this knowledge in this respect is not false.

As for the lie, it does not necessarily follow, because he mentioned his saying "Indeed, I am ill" by way of allusion, meaning that a person in most of his states is never free from some disliked condition, either in his body or in his heart, and all of that is sickness.

I said to some of them: This hadith should not be accepted, because attributing a lie to Abraham is not permissible. That man said: Then how is it judged that the reliable narrators lied? I said: When there was a contradiction between attributing a lie to the narrator and attributing it to the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, it was known by necessity that attributing it to the narrator is more fitting. Then we say: Why is it not permissible that the intended meaning of its being a lie is a statement resembling a lie?

The eighth answer: The intended meaning of His saying "Then he glanced a glance at the stars" is: he looked into the stars of their speech and their scattered statements, for things that occur piece by piece are called "munajjama" (scattered), that is, dispersed, and from it comes "nujum al-kitabah" (installments of writing). The meaning is that when he heard their scattered words, he looked into them in order to draw from them a stratagem by which he could establish an excuse for himself for staying behind from them. He found no better excuse than his saying: "Indeed, I am ill." The meaning is that he must indeed become ill, just as you say to someone you see at the times of travel: "You are a traveler."

Know that when Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, I am ill," they turned away from him, leaving him, and they excused him from going out that day, and that was his intention. ﴿Then he slipped away to their gods﴾: it is said "raagha ilayhi" when one inclines toward something secretly, by way of concealment, and from it comes "rawaghan al-tha'lab" (the fox's sly sidling). His saying "Will you not eat?" means the food that was before them, and he said that mockingly toward them. Likewise His saying: "What is wrong with you that you do not speak?" ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking﴾: he came upon them covertly, as if he said: "So he struck them with a blow," because "raagha 'alayhim" has the sense of "darabahum" (he struck them), or "fara'a 'alayhim darban" means "striking" (dhariban). Regarding His saying "with the right hand" there are two views:

The first: It means with strength and force, because the right hand is the stronger of the two limbs.

The second: He performed that act because of an oath, which is His saying, exalted is He, quoted from him: ﴿By Allah, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. Then He said: ﴿Then they came toward him, hastening.﴾ Hamzah recited "yuzaffunna" with a dammah on the yaa', and the others with a fatha, and both are dialects. Ibn 'Arafah said: Whoever reads with fatha, it is from "zaffa yaziffu", and whoever reads with damma, it is from "azaffa yuzifu". Al-Zajjaj said: "yazaffuna" means they hasten, and its origin is from the zafif of the ostrich, which is the beginning of its running. And Hamzah's reading "yuzaffunna" means they bring others to hasten, meaning they drive others to rush. Al-Asma'i said: It is said "azfaftu al-ibil" when you drive the camels to hasten, and he said: it is the quickness of step and near-running walk, and the object is omitted in his reading, as if they made their animals hasten in walking. This implies that at first they did not know him, so there is a contradiction between these two verses? We say: It is not far-fetched to say that a group of them knew him and rushed toward him, while most of them did not know him, so they then learned who that breaker was. And Allah knows best.

The second story: the story of Abraham, peace be upon him.

The first issue: To what does the pronoun in His saying "from his followers" (min shi'atihi) refer? There are two opinions:

The first, and the most apparent, is that it refers to Noah, peace be upon him, meaning: from the followers of Noah, that is, from his family and upon his religion and method, [was] Abraham. They said: Between Noah and Abraham there were only two prophets, Hud and Salih. The author of al-Kashshaf narrated that between Noah and Abraham there were two thousand six hundred and forty years.

The second: al-Kalbi said: The intended meaning is from the followers of Muhammad, ﷺ, [applied] to Abraham, in the sense that he was upon his religion and method, so he is among his followers even though he preceded him. The first is more apparent, because the mention of Noah, peace be upon him, came earlier, and the mention of the Prophet ﷺ did not come earlier, so returning the pronoun to Noah is preferable.

The second issue: The governing element of "when" (idh) is what is indicated by His saying "among his followers" (min shi'atihi), from the sense of following, meaning: and indeed among those who followed him in his religion and piety, at the time when he came to his Lord with a sound heart, [was] Abraham.

As for His saying "when he came to his Lord with a sound heart," there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning His saying "with a sound heart," there are two opinions:

The first: Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: It means pure from polytheism; the meaning is that he was free from shirk, so he did not associate partners with Allah.

The second: The scholars of usul (legal theory) said: The intended meaning is that he lived and died upon the purity of the heart from every defilement of sins, so it includes his being free from shirk, from doubt, from rancor, deceit, spite and envy.

From Ibn Abbas: he used to love for people what he loved for himself, and all people were safe from his deceit and his injustice; and Allah made him submit, so He did not equate anyone with Him. Those who held the first opinion argued that after this phrase He mentioned his denunciation of his people's shirk with Allah, which is His saying: "When he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'" Those who held the second opinion argued that the wording is absolute, so it is not restricted by one attribute rather than another, and this is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already given Abraham his right guidance before, and We were knowing of him.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 51]. Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124], and He said: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain [in faith].﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. If it is asked: what is the meaning of "coming to his Lord with his heart"? We say: its meaning is that he sincerely dedicated his heart to Allah, so it is as if he presented that heart as a gift to the presence of Allah. I have seen in the Torah that Allah said to Moses: "Answer your God with all your heart."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that Abraham came to his Lord with a sound heart, He mentioned that among the effects of that soundness was that he called his father and his people to monotheism, saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ The purpose of this speech is to disparage that way and to condemn it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ifkan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), its implied form being: "Do you desire gods other than Him as a falsehood?" He placed the object before the verb for emphasis, and placed the object of purpose before the direct object, because it was more important to him that he establish before them that they were in falsehood and vanity in their polytheism. It is also permissible that "ifkan" is a direct object, meaning: "Do you desire a falsehood?" Then he explained the falsehood by His saying: "gods other than Allah," as being falsehood in themselves. It is also permissible that it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Do you desire gods other than Allah as liars?"

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ On this there are two views:
One: Do you think of the Lord of the worlds that it is permissible to make these inanimate things partners to Him in worship?

Second: Do you think of the Lord of the worlds that He is of the same kind as these bodies, such that you made them equal to Him in worship? Thereby He alerted them that "there is nothing like unto Him."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then he glanced at the stars.﴾ ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ From Ibn Abbas: they used to engage in the knowledge of the stars, so he dealt with them according to their customary practice. The reason is that he intended to outwit them regarding their idols, to compel them to the proof that they are not worthy of worship. The next day was a festival day for them when they would go out, so he wished to stay behind from them, to remain alone in the house of the idols, so that he could break them. Here there are two questions:

The first: Studying the knowledge of the stars is not permissible, so how did Abraham undertake it?

The second: He, peace be upon him, was not ill, so when he said "Indeed, I am ill," was that a lie? Know that the scholars mentioned many answers to these two:

The first: He glanced a glance at the stars at times of night and day, and a sickness such as fever would come upon him at certain hours of night and day, so he looked to know whether it was at that hour, and said: "Indeed, I am ill," making it an excuse for staying behind from the festival they had. He was truthful in what he said, because the sickness used to come upon him at that time, and he stayed behind only for the sake of breaking their idols.

The second answer: The people of Abraham, peace be upon him, were masters of the stars; they glorified them and judged by them concerning unseen matters. Therefore Abraham looked at the stars, that is, into the sciences of the stars and their meanings, not that he looked at them with his own eyes. It is like saying: "So-and-so looked into jurisprudence and grammar." He only wanted to make them think that he knew what they knew and understood from the same sources they understood, so that when he said "Indeed, I am ill," they would rest content with his words.

As for His saying "Indeed, I am ill," its meaning is: "I will become ill," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die﴾ [az-Zumar: 30], that is, you will die.

The third answer: His saying "Then he glanced at the stars" refers to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star﴾ [al-An'am: 76], and so on through the verses. That glance was in order to learn the states of these stars, whether they are eternal or originated. And his saying "Indeed, I am ill" means: sick of heart, not knowing my Lord. And that was before puberty.

The fourth answer: Ibn Zayd said: He had a particular star, and whenever it rose in a particular configuration, Abraham would fall ill. By this induction, when he saw it rising in that particular configuration at that time, he said: "Indeed, I am ill," meaning: this sickness is certainly going to occur.

The fifth answer: His saying "Indeed, I am ill" means: sick of heart, because of that great multitude's unanimity upon disbelief and polytheism. Allah, exalted is He, said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 3].

The sixth answer: We do not concede that studying the knowledge of the stars and reasoning by comparing them is forbidden, because whoever believes that Allah, exalted is He, has specified each of these stars with a power and a property for which a particular effect appears from it, this knowledge in this respect is not false.

As for the lie, it does not necessarily follow, because he mentioned his saying "Indeed, I am ill" by way of allusion, meaning that a person in most of his states is never free from some disliked condition, either in his body or in his heart, and all of that is sickness.

I said to some of them: This hadith should not be accepted, because attributing a lie to Abraham is not permissible. That man said: Then how is it judged that the reliable narrators lied? I said: When there was a contradiction between attributing a lie to the narrator and attributing it to the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, it was known by necessity that attributing it to the narrator is more fitting. Then we say: Why is it not permissible that the intended meaning of its being a lie is a statement resembling a lie?

The eighth answer: The intended meaning of His saying "Then he glanced a glance at the stars" is: he looked into the stars of their speech and their scattered statements, for things that occur piece by piece are called "munajjama" (scattered), that is, dispersed, and from it comes "nujum al-kitabah" (installments of writing). The meaning is that when he heard their scattered words, he looked into them in order to draw from them a stratagem by which he could establish an excuse for himself for staying behind from them. He found no better excuse than his saying: "Indeed, I am ill." The meaning is that he must indeed become ill, just as you say to someone you see at the times of travel: "You are a traveler."

Know that when Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, I am ill," they turned away from him, leaving him, and they excused him from going out that day, and that was his intention. ﴿Then he slipped away to their gods﴾: it is said "raagha ilayhi" when one inclines toward something secretly, by way of concealment, and from it comes "rawaghan al-tha'lab" (the fox's sly sidling). His saying "Will you not eat?" means the food that was before them, and he said that mockingly toward them. Likewise His saying: "What is wrong with you that you do not speak?" ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking﴾: he came upon them covertly, as if he said: "So he struck them with a blow," because "raagha 'alayhim" has the sense of "darabahum" (he struck them), or "fara'a 'alayhim darban" means "striking" (dhariban). Regarding His saying "with the right hand" there are two views:

The first: It means with strength and force, because the right hand is the stronger of the two limbs.

The second: He performed that act because of an oath, which is His saying, exalted is He, quoted from him: ﴿By Allah, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. Then He said: ﴿Then they came toward him, hastening.﴾ Hamzah recited "yuzaffunna" with a dammah on the yaa', and the others with a fatha, and both are dialects. We say: It is not far-fetched to say that a group of them knew him and rushed toward him, while most of them did not know him, so they then learned who that breaker was. And Allah knows best.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ ﴿And Allah created you and what you do.﴾ ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire."﴾ ﴿They intended a scheme against him, but We made them the lowest.﴾ ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ ﴿"My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous."﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾** In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when the people blamed Abraham for breaking the idols, he also presented to them the proof that shows the corruption of turning to worship them. So he said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve? And Allah created you and what you do.﴾ The mode of argument is clear: wood and stone, before being carved and shaped, were never at all an object of worship for man. When he carves it and shapes it in a particular form, nothing arises in it except the traces of his handiwork. So if it became an object of worship at that point, the meaning would be that a thing which was not worshipped, once the traces of human action appeared in it, became worshipped at that point. The falsity of this is known by the immediate judgment of reason.

**The second issue:** The majority of our companions (aṣḥābunā, i.e., the Ash'arī scholars) argued with His saying, ﴿And Allah created you and what you do,﴾ that the act of the servant is created by Allah, Exalted is He. The grammarians (al-naḥwiyyūn) said: they agreed that the word *mā* (what) together with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar). So His saying ﴿and what you do﴾ means "and your doing." On this reading the meaning of the verse becomes: "And Allah created you and created your doing."

If it is said: this verse is a proof against you in several respects:

*First:* He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ He attributed the worship and the carving to them, attributing the act to the agent. If that were occurring by the creation of Allah, it would be impossible for it to be an act of the servant.

*Second:* He, Exalted is He, mentioned this verse only as a rebuke to them for worshipping idols, because He, Exalted is He, made clear that He is their Creator and the Creator of those idols. The Creator is the one deserving worship, not the created. So when they abandoned the worship of Him, Glorified is He, though He is their Creator, and worshipped idols, He, Glorified and Exalted is He, rebuked them for this great error, saying: ﴿Do you worship what you carve? And Allah created you and what you do.﴾ If they were not the agents of their own actions, the rebuke for them would not be valid.

We grant that this verse is not a proof against you; but we do not grant that it is a proof for you. As for your claim that the word *mā* together with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun, we say: this is disputed. Its explanation is that Sibawayh and al-Akhfash disagreed about whether one may say, "I was pleased by *mā qumta*," meaning "by your standing up." Sibawayh permitted it and al-Akhfash prohibited it, and he claimed that this is not permitted except with a transitive verb. This indicates that *mā* together with what follows it is, according to al-Akhfash, in the sense of an object (maf'ūl). Know that when he, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, emigrated to the holy land, he desired offspring and said: ﴿Grant me [a son] from among the righteous.﴾ That is: grant me some of the righteous, meaning a son; because the word *hibah* (gift) has become predominantly used for a son, though it has also come for a brother in His saying: ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.﴾ [Maryam: 53], and He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ [al-An'ām: 84], ﴿And We gave him Yahyā﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 90]. And 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib said to Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he congratulated him on his son: "You thanked the Giver for the sake of the father of the gifts, and blessing was placed in what was given to you." For this reason, names were formed as "Gift of Allah," "Gift of the Bestower," and "Given" and "Gift-given" (Mawhūb and Wahb).

Know that this supplication included three things: that the child would be a male boy, that he would reach the age of maturity, and that he would be forbearing. And what forbearance is greater than that of a son who, when his father proposed to slaughter him, said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient.﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 102], then submitted to that. Also, Abraham, peace be upon him, was described with forbearance; He said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114], and ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and penitent﴾ [Hūd: 75]. So He made clear that his son was described with forbearance, and that he stood in his station in the qualities of nobility and excellence. Know that righteousness is the best of qualities, as evidenced by the fact that the Friend (Khalīl), peace be upon him, sought righteousness for himself, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 83]; and he sought it for his offspring, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous.﴾ And Solomon, peace be upon him, sought it after the perfection of his rank in religion and worldly affairs, saying: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ [al-Naml: 19]. This indicates that righteousness is the most noble of the stations of the servants.

[Page 133]

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾

Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to proceed to carry out the command and not to consult the son about it, and not to say to him, ﴿so see what you think﴾, and not to suspend the action until the son said to him, ﴿do as you are commanded﴾? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. If it is the second, namely that it was not established by proof among them that what they see in dreams is true, then how is it permissible for him to proceed to slaughter that child merely on the basis of a vision for which no proof indicates that it is binding? The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They differed about who this sacrificed one was. It was said: he was Isaac. This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Ibn Masʿūd, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Qatādah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, and Muqātil, may Allah be pleased with them. And it was said: he was Ismāʿīl. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī,
[Page 134]
Mujāhid, and al-Kalbī. Those who argued that it was Ismāʿīl gave several arguments:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And a Bedouin said to him, "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him, "Ransom your son with a hundred camels," and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. And the second sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl.

The second argument: It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Aṣmaʿī, where is your reason? When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:
[Page 135]
﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.
