It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:
[Page 135]
﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

[Page 133]

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾

Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to proceed to carry out the command and not to consult the son about it, and not to say to him, ﴿so see what you think﴾, and not to suspend the action until the son said to him, ﴿do as you are commanded﴾? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. If it is the second, namely that it was not established by proof among them that what they see in dreams is true, then how is it permissible for him to proceed to slaughter that child merely on the basis of a vision for which no proof indicates that it is binding? The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

[Page 133]

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾

Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to proceed to carry out the command and not to consult the son about it, and not to say to him, ﴿so see what you think﴾, and not to suspend the action until the son said to him, ﴿do as you are commanded﴾? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. If it is the second, namely that it was not established by proof among them that what they see in dreams is true, then how is it permissible for him to proceed to slaughter that child merely on the basis of a vision for which no proof indicates that it is binding? The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They differed about who this sacrificed one was. It was said: he was Isaac. This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Ibn Masʿūd, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Qatādah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, and Muqātil, may Allah be pleased with them. And it was said: he was Ismāʿīl. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī,
[Page 134]
Mujāhid, and al-Kalbī. Those who argued that it was Ismāʿīl gave several arguments:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And a Bedouin said to him, "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him, "Ransom your son with a hundred camels," and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. And the second sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl.

The second argument: It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Aṣmaʿī, where is your reason? When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:
[Page 135]
﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

And a Bedouin said to him, "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him, "Ransom your son with a hundred camels," and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. And the second sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl.

The second argument: It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Aṣmaʿī, where is your reason? When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:
[Page 135]
﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

[Page 133]

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾

Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to proceed to carry out the command and not to consult the son about it, and not to say to him, ﴿so see what you think﴾, and not to suspend the action until the son said to him, ﴿do as you are commanded﴾? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. If it is the second, namely that it was not established by proof among them that what they see in dreams is true, then how is it permissible for him to proceed to slaughter that child merely on the basis of a vision for which no proof indicates that it is binding? The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Rather, it would have been obligatory for him to proceed to carry out the command and not to consult the son about it, and not to say to him, ﴿so see what you think﴾, and not to suspend the action until the son said to him, ﴿do as you are commanded﴾? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. If it is the second, namely that it was not established by proof among them that what they see in dreams is true, then how is it permissible for him to proceed to slaughter that child merely on the basis of a vision for which no proof indicates that it is binding? The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They differed about who this sacrificed one was. It was said: he was Isaac. This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Ibn Masʿūd, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Qatādah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, and Muqātil, may Allah be pleased with them. And it was said: he was Ismāʿīl. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī,

Mujāhid, and al-Kalbī. Those who argued that it was Ismāʿīl gave several arguments:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And a Bedouin said to him, "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him, "Ransom your son with a hundred camels," and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. And the second sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl.

The second argument: It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Aṣmaʿī, where is your reason? When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.
