The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

The answer: it is not far-fetched to say that he was hesitant about it at the time of the vision, then the vision was confirmed by explicit revelation. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They differed about who this sacrificed one was. It was said: he was Isaac. This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Ibn Masʿūd, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Qatādah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, and Muqātil, may Allah be pleased with them. And it was said: he was Ismāʿīl. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī,
[Page 134]
Mujāhid, and al-Kalbī. Those who argued that it was Ismāʿīl gave several arguments:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And a Bedouin said to him, "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, and he was asked about that, and he said: When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib dug the well of Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so his maternal uncles prevented him and said to him, "Ransom your son with a hundred camels," and he ransomed him with a hundred camels. And the second sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl.

The second argument: It is reported from al-Aṣmaʿī that he said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Aṣmaʿī, where is your reason? When was Isaac in Mecca? It was Ismāʿīl who was in Mecca, and he is the one who built the House with his father and the place of sacrifice at Mecca."

The third argument: Allah described Ismāʿīl with steadfastness rather than Isaac, in His saying: ﴿And Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, each of them was among the steadfast﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 85], and this steadfastness is his patience in the face of slaughter. He also described him with truthfulness of promise, in His saying: ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father of his own accord to be patient in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it.

The fourth argument: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hūd: 71]. We say: if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then the command to slaughter him would either have occurred before Jacob was born from him, or after that. The first is invalid, because when He gave her good news of Isaac, and with him gave good news that Jacob would come from him, then before Jacob was born from him it was not permissible for the command to slaughter him, otherwise there would be a contradiction in His saying: ﴿and after Isaac﴾. The second is also invalid, because His saying: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾ indicates that when that son became able to exert himself and reached the limit of ability to act, Allah commanded Abraham to slaughter him, and this contradicts the occurrence of this story at another time. Thus it is established that the sacrificed one cannot be Isaac.

The fifth argument: Allah related of him that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 99], then he asked Allah for a child to keep him company in his exile, and he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 100]. This request is appropriate only before he had a child, because if he had one child, he would not ask for one child, since asking for what one already has is impossible. And His saying: ﴿grant me of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child, and the particle "min" (of) is for partitive meaning, and the least degree of partiality is one. So His saying: ﴿of the righteous﴾ implies only the request for one child. Thus it is established that this request is appropriate only when all children are absent, and so it is established that this request occurred when he was seeking his first child. People are agreed that Ismāʿīl preceded Isaac in existence, so it is established that the one sought by this supplication was Ismāʿīl. Then Allah mentioned the story of the sacrificed one right after it, so it is necessary that the sacrificed one be Ismāʿīl.

The sixth argument: the many reports about the ram's horn being hung at the Kaʿbah, so the sacrificed one was at Mecca. And if the sacrificed one had been Isaac, the sacrifice would have been in Syria.

Those who said that the sacrificed one was Isaac argued with two points:

The first point: the beginning and the end of the verse indicate this. As for its beginning: before this verse, Allah related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, and they agree that what is meant by it is his migration to Syria. Then He said: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, so it is necessary that this boy is none other than Isaac. Then He said after it: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾, and this requires that the one meant by this boy who reached the age of exertion with him is that boy who was born in Syria. Thus it is established that the opening of this verse indicates that the sacrificed one is Isaac. As for the end of the verse, it too indicates this, because when He had completed the story of the sacrificed one, He said after it:
[Page 135]
﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Its meaning is that He gave him the good news of his being a prophet from among the righteous. Mentioning this good news right after the narration of that story indicates that Allah gave him this prophethood only because he had borne these hardships in the story of the sacrificed one. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that the beginning and the end of the verse indicate that the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The second point: in support of this is what is well known from the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon him: "From Jacob, Israel, the prophet of Allah, son of Isaac, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Abraham, the friend of Allah." This is the sum of what is said on this subject. Al-Zajjāj used to say: "Allah knows best which of the two is the sacrificed one." And Allah knows best.

Know also that the disagreement about the place of the sacrifice branches out from what we have mentioned. Those who said the sacrificed one is Ismāʿīl said: the sacrifice was at Minā. Those who said it is Isaac said: it was in Syria, and it was said: at Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: People differed as to whether Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this by what he saw. This disagreement is based on an issue of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh), namely whether it is permissible to abrogate a ruling (naskh) before the period for carrying it out has arrived. Most of our companions said that it is permissible. The Muʿtazilah and many jurists of the Shāfiʿīs and the Ḥanafīs said that it is not permissible. On the first view, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, commanded him to slaughter, then Allah abrogated this obligation before the time for it had come. On the second view, Allah did not command him to slaughter; rather He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter. This is a noble issue among the issues of the chapter on abrogation (bāb al-naskh). Our companions argued that it is permissible to abrogate a command before the period for compliance has come, by saying that Allah commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son, then Allah abrogated it from him before he proceeded to do it, and this serves the point. We said that He commanded him to slaughter the son for two reasons:

The first: he, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you." The son said: "Do as you are commanded," and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to the preliminaries of slaughter, not to the slaughter itself. Then he carried out the preliminaries of slaughter and brought them into existence, and at that point he would have been commanded with something and would have done it, and at this point he would not need a ransom. But he did need a ransom, based on His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 107]. This shows that he had carried out what he was commanded, and it has been established that he carried out all the preliminaries of slaughter, and this indicates that Allah had commanded him with the slaughter itself. Once this is established, we say that Allah abrogated that ruling before it was established, and this supports the point. The Muʿtazilah said: We do not grant that Allah commanded him to slaughter the son; rather we say that He commanded him to the preliminaries of slaughter, and several points indicate this:

The first point: he did not actually carry out the slaughter. He only did the preliminaries to the slaughter. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that
Page 137
dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

[Page 133]

ﷻ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ [Page 133 continues] ﴿"Peace upon Abraham.﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he is among Our believing servants."﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾

Know that when Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, said, ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy,﴾ He followed it with what indicates the attainment of what he had been given good news of and his reaching maturity, so He said, ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾. Its meaning: when he reached and attained the limit at which he was able to exert himself. His saying, ﴿with him﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the implied sense is "being with him." The benefit of considering this meaning is that a father is the most gentle of people toward his child, whereas others may be harsh with him in demanding effort, and so he would not bear it, because his strength had not yet become firm. Some have said: at that time he was thirteen years old. The purpose of this statement is that when Allah, Exalted is He, promised him in the first verse that this boy would be forbearing, this verse made clear what indicates the perfection of his forbearance, because he possessed such perfection of forbearance and breadth of heart that strengthened him to bear that great trial and to give that good answer.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: In interpreting this expression there are two views.

The first: al-Suddi said: when Abraham was given the good news of Isaac before he had been born to him, he said, "Then he will be a sacrifice for Allah." It was said to Abraham, "You have made a vow, so fulfill your vow." When morning came, ﴿he said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾

It has been narrated by another route that on the night of Tarwiyah he saw in his dream as if someone said to him, "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When morning came, he deliberated on this from the morning until the afternoon: was this vision from Allah or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). When evening came, he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from Allah, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafah (recognition). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). This is the view of the scholars of tafsir.

This indicates that he saw in his dream what required that he slaughter his son in waking reality. On this view, the wording is to be understood as: "Indeed I see in a dream what requires that I slaughter you."

The second view: he saw in a dream that he was slaughtering him. The visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are a form of revelation. On this view, what was seen in the dream was nothing other than that he was slaughtering him. If it is said: either it is established by proof for the prophets, peace be upon them, that everything they see in a dream is true and binding, or it is not established by proof among them. If it is the first, then why did he consult the son in this matter? Also, you have said that he remained in contemplation on the first day; if it had been established for him by proof that everything he saw in sleep was true, there would have been no need for this deliberation and reflection. Then God informed us that he did what he had been commanded, as shown by His words: ﴿And We called out to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ This indicates that God commanded him in the dream only to perform the preliminaries of slaughter, not the slaughter itself. These preliminaries are his laying the son down, placing the knife on his throat, and the sound resolve to do that act if the command were to come.

The second point: slaughter is the cutting of the windpipe (al-ḥulqūm). Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, did cut the windpipe, but every time he cut a part, God restored the joining of the tissue to it. For this reason, death did not occur.

The third point, on which the scholars rely: if God commands a specific person to perform a specific act at a specific time, this indicates that performing that act at that time is good. If He then forbids him from it, that prohibition indicates that performing that act at that time is bad. If this prohibition came immediately after that command, one of two things would follow. If God knew the state of that act, it would follow that He commanded what is evil or forbade what is good. If He did not know it, it would follow that God is ignorant, which is impossible. This is the full discussion of this topic.

As for the answer to the first point: we have already shown that God commanded him to slaughter.

As for His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, this indicates that he acknowledged that the vision was binding to act upon. It does not indicate that he did everything he saw in that dream.

As for his second claim, that every time Abraham, peace be upon him, cut a part, God restored the joining to it: we say this is false. Had Abraham done everything he was commanded, he would not have needed the ransom (al-fidā'). Since he needed it, we know he did not do what he was commanded.

As for his third claim, that it necessarily follows either that a command to evil is given or that God is ignorant: we say this rests on the premise that God commands only what is good in itself and forbids only what is evil in itself. That premise rests on the doctrine of tahsin wa taqbih al-'aql (the position that reason itself determines what is good and evil), and that is false. Moreover, even if we grant that premise, we can still ask: why could it not be that a command to something is sometimes good because the thing commanded is good, and sometimes good because that command serves some benefit (maṣlaḥa), even if the thing commanded is not itself good? Do you not see that when a master wishes to train his slave, he may say to him, "When Friday comes, do such-and-such an act," and that act is one of the arduous tasks, and the master's purpose in that command is not that the slave actually perform that act, but that the slave accustom himself to obedience and submission. Then, when the master knows that the slave has accustomed himself to obedience, he may remove that burden and the pain from him. The same applies here. Unless you establish proof for the invalidity of this possibility, your argument is not complete.

Fourth issue: our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) used this verse to argue that God may command something He does not will to occur. The proof is that He commanded the slaughter, and He did not will its occurrence. That He commanded the slaughter is established from the previous issue. That He did not will its occurrence is because, according to us, whatever God wills to occur, occurs. Since this slaughter did not occur, we know that He did not will its occurrence. According to the Mu'tazilah, the proof is that God forbade that slaughter, and a prohibition of something indicates that the one prohibiting does not will its occurrence. Thus it is established that God commanded the slaughter, and it is established that He did not will it, and this indicates that a command may exist without the will. The full discussion of whether God commanded the slaughter was covered in the previous issue. And God knows best.

Fifth issue: explaining the wisdom in this obligation coming in a dream and not while awake. Its explanation has several aspects:

The first: this obligation was of the utmost hardship for both the slaughterer and the one slaughtered. So it came first in a dream, so that this would serve as a preparation for the arrival of this arduous obligation. Then the state of sleep is reinforced by the states of wakefulness, and at that point this obligation does not descend all at once, but gradually.

The second: God made the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, true. God said regarding Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿God certainly fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. He said of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. And He said regarding Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The purpose of this is to strengthen the evidence that they were truthful, because the state is either a state of wakefulness or a state of sleep. When both states agree on truthfulness, that is the ultimate demonstration that they were rightly guided and truthful in all conditions. And God knows best.

Then we say: the stations of the prophets, peace be upon them, are of three kinds:

Among them is that which occurs in accordance with the vision, as in His words regarding our Messenger ﷺ: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and then that very thing occurred.

Among them is that which occurs in the opposite way, as with Abraham, peace be upon him: he saw the slaughter, but what resulted was the ransom and the deliverance.

Among them is that which occurs through some kind of interpretation and correspondence, as with the vision of Joseph, peace be upon him. For this reason, the people of dream interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'bīr) agreed that

dreams come to pass in these three ways.

Sixth issue: Hamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿turī﴾ with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning "what you show of yourself" of patience and submission. It was also said it means "what you indicate." The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā', and among them some use imālah (a vowel-leaning pronunciation) and some do not.

Seventh issue: The wisdom in consulting the son in this matter is to inform his son of this event so that his patience in obeying God would become apparent to him. Thus Abraham would find comfort in him, seeing that he had reached such a great level of forbearance and such a high degree of patience in the face of the most severe hardships. And the son would attain great reward in the Hereafter and a good reputation in this world. Then God related from Abraham's son, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. Its meaning: do what you are commanded to do. The preposition was omitted, as it is omitted in the line of poetry:

"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded [with]."

Then he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ He attached this to God's will only as a means of seeking blessing and good omen, and to affirm that there is no turning away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no power to obey God except by God's enabling.

Then God Most High said: ﴿So when they had both submitted﴾. It is said: sallama li-amr Allah (he submitted to the command of God), aslama (he surrendered) and istaslama (he yielded) have one meaning, and all three have been recited thus, when he yielded to Him and humbled himself. Its origin is from your saying "salima hadha li-fulan" (this became pure/secure for so-and-so) when it was exclusively his, and its meaning is that it was safe from being disputed over. The saying "sallama li-amr Allah" and "aslama lahu" are both transmitted with the hamza (causative form). The real meaning of these is that he made his self exclusively for God and made it safe and pure for Him, and likewise the meaning of istaslama is that he made his self exclusive to God. And it is transmitted from Qatadah regarding aslama: "Aslama" means this one (Abraham) submitted his son, and this one (the son) submitted himself.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And He threw him down upon his forehead﴾, that is, he threw him down on his side so that one of his two temples fell upon the ground. The face has two temples (jabinan), and the brow lies between them. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-talil and al-matlul are the one thrown down, and al-mitall is that by which one is thrown down, i.e. one is struck down. So the meaning is that He threw him down upon his temple. Muqatil said: "He overturned him onto his forehead," and this is an error, because the temple (jabin) is not the forehead (jabhah).

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿And We called to him: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾. Regarding this there are two views:
The first: this is the response (jawab) to "falamma" according to the Kufans and al-Farra', and the waw is superfluous.

The second view: according to the Basrans this is not permissible, and the response is implied. The estimate is: "When he did that and God called to him, 'O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision,' he attained a great felicity, God gave him prophethood for his son, and He greatly rewarded him." They said: omitting the response is not uncommon in the Qur'an, and the benefit of it is that when it is omitted it is greater and more majestic. The commentators said: When he laid him down for slaughter, he was called from the mountain: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the reason for this trial was the perfection of Abraham's obedience to the commands of God Most High. When God imposed upon him this arduous, severe obligation, and perfect obedience appeared from him, and perfect obedience and submission appeared from his son, He therefore said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, meaning the purpose of that vision was achieved.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ is the beginning of a statement from God Most High, and it is not connected to what preceded in speech. The meaning is that Abraham and his son were both doers of good in this obedience; just as We rewarded these two good-doers, so likewise We reward all good-doers.

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial﴾, that is, the manifest test by which the sincere are distinguished from others, or the evident trial whose difficulty is such that no trial is harder than it. ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Dhabh (the act of slaughter) is the verbal noun of dhabaḥtu, and dhibh is also what is slaughtered, and this is what is meant in this verse. Here there are discussions related to the narratives:

The first: It is related in the story of the sacrificed son that when Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to slaughter him, he said: "My son, take the rope and the knife and let us go to the ravine to gather firewood." When they reached the middle of the ravine of Thabir, he informed him of what he had been commanded. He said: "Father, tighten my bonds upon me so that I do not thrash, and keep your garments away from me so that nothing of my blood splashes upon them and your wife sees it and grieves, and sharpen your blade and hasten its passage over my throat so that it will be easier, for death is severe, and convey my greetings to my mother, and if you see fit to return my shirt to my mother, do so, for perhaps it will be easier for her." Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "What an excellent helper you are, my son, in the matter of God's command." Then he turned to him, kissing him, while he had bound him, and both were weeping. Then he placed the knife upon his throat, and he said: "Lay me down on my face, for when you look at my face you will have mercy upon me and tenderness will overcome you, and it may come between you and the command of God, glorified and exalted be He." He did so, then he placed the knife upon his nape, and the knife turned over, and it was called: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."

The second discussion: They differed concerning that ram. It was said that it is the ram with which Abel, son of Adam, drew near to God Most High, and He accepted it, and it was in Paradise grazing until God Most High ransomed Ishmael with it. Others said: God sent a ram from Paradise which had grazed for forty autumns. Al-Suddi said: Abraham was called, and he turned, and behold, there was a white-black ram (amlah) descending from the mountain; Abraham rose from him, took it, slaughtered it, and let go of his son; then he embraced his son and said: "My son, today you have been given to me." As for His saying: ﴿great﴾, it was said that it was called great for its greatness and fatness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it deserved to be great, for it had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns. It was also said it was called great for the greatness of its rank, since God Most High accepted it as a ransom for Abraham's son. Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾. The pronoun in His saying "innahu" refers to Abraham. Then God Most High said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. His saying "nabiyyan" is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is anticipated (muqaddarah), meaning: We gave him the good news of Isaac's existence, his prophethood being anticipated. For whoever says the sacrificed one is Ishmael, there is an argument from this verse, because His saying "nabiyyan" is a circumstantial clause, and it is not permissible that the meaning be "and We gave him the good news of Isaac while Isaac was a prophet," since the good news of him preceded his becoming a prophet. Therefore the meaning must be "and We gave him the good news of Isaac at the time We had decreed him a prophet, and at the time We had judged regarding him, so he endured." If this is so, then this good news of Isaac's existence occurred after the story of the sacrificed one, and therefore the sacrificed one must not be Isaac. At most one could say: it is not unlikely that this verse, though later in recitation than the story of the sacrificed one, preceded it in occurrence and existence. But we say: the principle is to observe the order and not to alter the arrangement in the text. And God knows best what is correct.

The real meaning of these is that he made his self exclusively for God and made it safe and pure for Him, and likewise the meaning of istaslama is that he made his self exclusive to God. And it is transmitted from Qatadah regarding aslama: "Aslama" means this one (Abraham) submitted his son, and this one (the son) submitted himself.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And He threw him down upon his forehead﴾, that is, he threw him down on his side so that one of his two temples fell upon the ground. The face has two temples (jabinan), and the brow lies between them. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-talil and al-matlul are the one thrown down, and al-mitall is that by which one is thrown down, i.e. one is struck down. So the meaning is that He threw him down upon his temple. Muqatil said: "He overturned him onto his forehead," and this is an error, because the temple (jabin) is not the forehead (jabhah).

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿And We called to him: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾. Regarding this there are two views:
The first: this is the response (jawab) to "falamma" according to the Kufans and al-Farra', and the waw is superfluous.

The second view: according to the Basrans this is not permissible, and the response is implied. The estimate is: "When he did that and God called to him, 'O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision,' he attained a great felicity, God gave him prophethood for his son, and He greatly rewarded him." They said: omitting the response is not uncommon in the Qur'an, and the benefit of it is that when it is omitted it is greater and more majestic. The commentators said: When he laid him down for slaughter, he was called from the mountain: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the reason for this trial was the perfection of Abraham's obedience to the commands of God Most High. When God imposed upon him this arduous, severe obligation, and perfect obedience appeared from him, and perfect obedience and submission appeared from his son, He therefore said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾, meaning the purpose of that vision was achieved.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ is the beginning of a statement from God Most High, and it is not connected to what preceded in speech. The meaning is that Abraham and his son were both doers of good in this obedience; just as We rewarded these two good-doers, so likewise We reward all good-doers.

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial﴾, that is, the manifest test by which the sincere are distinguished from others, or the evident trial whose difficulty is such that no trial is harder than it. ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Dhabh (the act of slaughter) is the verbal noun of dhabaḥtu, and dhibh is also what is slaughtered, and this is what is meant in this verse. Here there are discussions related to the narratives:

The first: It is related in the story of the sacrificed son that when Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to slaughter him, he said: "My son, take the rope and the knife and let us go to the ravine to gather firewood." When they reached the middle of the ravine of Thabir, he informed him of what he had been commanded. He said: "Father, tighten my bonds upon me so that I do not thrash, and keep your garments away from me so that nothing of my blood splashes upon them and your wife sees it and grieves, and sharpen your blade and hasten its passage over my throat so that it will be easier, for death is severe, and convey my greetings to my mother, and if you see fit to return my shirt to my mother, do so, for perhaps it will be easier for her." Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "What an excellent helper you are, my son, in the matter of God's command." Then he turned to him, kissing him, while he had bound him, and both were weeping. Then he placed the knife upon his throat, and he said: "Lay me down on my face, for when you look at my face you will have mercy upon me and tenderness will overcome you, and it may come between you and the command of God, glorified and exalted be He." He did so, then he placed the knife upon his nape, and the knife turned over, and it was called: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."

The second discussion: They differed concerning that ram. It was said that it is the ram with which Abel, son of Adam, drew near to God Most High, and He accepted it, and it was in Paradise grazing until God Most High ransomed Ishmael with it. Others said: God sent a ram from Paradise which had grazed for forty autumns. Al-Suddi said: Abraham was called, and he turned, and behold, there was a white-black ram (amlah) descending from the mountain; Abraham rose from him, took it, slaughtered it, and let go of his son; then he embraced his son and said: "My son, today you have been given to me." As for His saying: ﴿great﴾, it was said that it was called great for its greatness and fatness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it deserved to be great, for it had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns. It was also said it was called great for the greatness of its rank, since God Most High accepted it as a ransom for Abraham's son. Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾. The pronoun in His saying "innahu" refers to Abraham. Then God Most High said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. His saying "nabiyyan" is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is anticipated (muqaddarah), meaning: We gave him the good news of Isaac's existence, his prophethood being anticipated. For whoever says the sacrificed one is Ishmael, there is an argument from this verse, because His saying "nabiyyan" is a circumstantial clause, and it is not permissible that the meaning be "and We gave him the good news of Isaac while Isaac was a prophet," since the good news of him preceded his becoming a prophet. Therefore the meaning must be "and We gave him the good news of Isaac at the time We had decreed him a prophet, and at the time We had judged regarding him, so he endured." If this is so, then this good news of Isaac's existence occurred after the story of the sacrificed one, and therefore the sacrificed one must not be Isaac. At most one could say: it is not unlikely that this verse, though later in recitation than the story of the sacrificed one, preceded it in occurrence and existence. But we say: the principle is to observe the order and not to alter the arrangement in the text. And God knows best what is correct.

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾. Regarding the interpretation of this blessing there are two views:
The first: God Most High brought forth all the prophets of the Children of Israel from the loins of Isaac.

The second: He preserved good praise for Abraham and Isaac until the Day of Resurrection, because blessing is an expression for permanence and stability. Then God Most High said: ﴿And among their offspring are one who does good and one who wrongs himself openly﴾. In this there is a notice that the abundance of the father's virtues does not necessarily entail the son's virtue, lest this doubt become a cause for the Jews' boasting. Included under His saying "one who does good" are the prophets and the believers, and included under His saying "one who wrongs" are the disbeliever and the transgressor. And God knows best.

The Story of Musa and Harun, peace be upon them

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor upon Musa and Harun﴾ ﴿And We delivered them and their people from the great distress﴾ ﴿And We helped them, so they were the victors﴾ ﴿And We gave them the clear Book﴾ ﴿And We guided them to the straight path﴾ ﴿And We left for them among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace upon Musa and Harun﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants﴾

Know that this is the third story among the stories mentioned in this surah. Know also that the aspects of blessing, although they are many, are confined to two kinds: bringing benefits to a person, and warding off harms from him. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned both kinds here. So His saying, ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor upon Musa and Harun﴾, points to bringing benefits to them, and His saying, ﴿And We delivered them and their people from the great distress﴾, points to warding off harms from them.

As for the first kind, bringing benefits, there is no doubt that benefits are of two kinds: worldly benefits and religious benefits. Worldly benefits are existence, life, intellect, upbringing, health, and the attainment of the attributes of perfection in the essence of each of them. Religious benefits are knowledge and obedience. The highest of these ranks is lofty prophethood accompanied by dazzling and overpowering miracles. Since Allah, exalted is He, mentioned these details in the rest of the surahs, He therefore was content here with this allusion.

As for the second kind, warding off harm, it is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And We delivered them and their people from the great distress﴾. Regarding it there are two views. It is said that it was drowning: Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people and saved the Children of Israel. It is also said that what is meant is that He, exalted is He, saved them from the harm of Pharaoh, since he used to slaughter their sons and let their women live.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He bestowed favor upon Musa and Harun, He detailed the categories of that favor. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿And We helped them﴾, refers to Musa, Harun and their people, meaning: We helped Musa and Harun and their people, ﴿so they were the victors﴾ in every circumstance through the manifestation of the proof, and in the end through sovereignty and exaltation.

The second of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave them the clear Book﴾, and what is meant by it is the Torah, which is the book comprising all the knowledge needed for the interests of religion and worldly life, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 44).

The third is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We guided them to the straight path﴾, meaning: We showed them the way of truth by reason and by revelation, and We supported them with success and protection from error. The likening of the sound proofs to the straight path is clear.

The fourth is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We left for them among later generations﴾, and regarding it there are two views:

The first: that what is meant by ﴿And We left for them among later generations﴾, namely the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), is their saying: ﴿Peace upon Musa and Harun﴾.

The second: that what is meant by ﴿And We left for them among later generations﴾, namely the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), is good praise and a beautiful remembrance. On this reading, His saying after that, ﴿Peace upon Musa and Harun﴾, is the speech of Allah, exalted is He. When He, exalted is He, mentioned these four categories of honour and preference, He said: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, and its explanation has already passed. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants﴾, and the intent is to draw attention to the fact that the virtue obtained through faith is more noble, higher and more complete than all other virtues. Were it not so, it would not have been fitting to conclude the virtues of Musa and Harun by stating that they were among the believers. And Allah knows best.

**The Story of Ilyas (peace be upon him)**

God the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed Ilyas was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators,﴾ ﴿God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old?﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth,﴾ ﴿except the sincere servants of God.﴾ ﴿And We left for him a good name among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon the family of Yasin."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾

Know that this is the fourth of the stories mentioned in this surah. It contains several issues.

**The First Issue:** Ibn 'Amir recited "Wa inna Ilyas" (وإنَّ الياسَ) without a hamza, with the alif pronounced as a connecting vowel (wasl). The rest of the readers recited it with a hamza and a cut alif (qat' al-alif). Abu Bakr ibn Mihran said: "Whoever pronounces the alif at the connection has made a mistake." The people of Syria rejected this reading and did not recognize it. Al-Wahidi said that it has two explanations:

The first is that he dropped the hamza from Ilyas entirely, as Ibn Kathir dropped it in the verse ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest [calamities]﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:35), and as in the words of the poet:

*"Woe to its mother, flying through the air, seeking..."*

The second is that he treated the hamza that accompanies the lam as the definite article, as in the verse ﴿and Elisha (al-Yasa')﴾ (al-An'am 6:86).

**The Second Issue:** There are two opinions concerning Ilyas. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Wa inna Idris" (وإنَّ إدْرِيسَ) and said that Ilyas is Idris. This is also the view of 'Ikrimah. However, most commentators agree that he was a prophet from among the prophets of the Children of Israel, and that he is Ilyas ibn Yasin, from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both.

Then God the Exalted says: ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear God?"﴾ The implied meaning is: "Mention, O Muhammad, to your people: when he said to his people, 'Will you not fear God?'" That is, "Will you not fear God?" Al-Kalbi said: "Will you not fear the worship of other than God?"

Know that when he first warned them in general terms, he then mentioned the cause of that fear, saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators﴾. There are several points here:

*The first point:* Concerning "Ba'l" (بَعْلٍ) there are two opinions:

The first is that it is the proper name of an idol that they had, like Manat and Hubal. It is said that it was made of gold, that its height was twenty cubits, and that it had four faces. They were enamored with it and glorified it so much that they appointed four hundred attendants for it and made them prophets. The devil would enter the belly of Ba'l and speak the law of error, and the attendants would memorize it and teach it to the people. They were the people of Ba'labakk in the lands of Syria, and their city was named after it, Ba'labakk. Know that their saying that Ba'l is the name of one of their idols is not objectionable. But their claim that the devil used to enter the belly of Ba'labakk and speak the law of error is problematic. For if we permit this, it would cast doubt on many of the miracles, since it is reported in the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ that a wolf spoke to him, a camel spoke to him, and a trunk (of a palm tree) moaned. If we allowed that the devil could enter the body of a creature and speak, then this possibility would also exist for the wolf, the camel, and the trunk, and that would undermine their being miracles.

The second opinion: Ba'l means "the Lord" in the language of Yemen. It is said, "Who is the ba'l of this house?" meaning, "Who is its lord?" The husband is called ba'l in this sense. God the Exalted says: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:228), and He says: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ (Hud 11:72). According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "Do you worship some lord other than God and abandon the worship of God?"

*The second point:* The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used this verse to argue that the servant creates his own actions. They said: If no one other than God were a creator, it would not be permissible to describe God as "the Best of Creators." The discussion of this has already been presented in His words: ﴿So blessed is God, the Best of Creators﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:14).

*The third point:* The one known as al-Rashid al-Katib used to say: "If it were said, 'Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators,' it would give the impression that [Ba'l] is the best, because there would be an observance of the sense of embellishment." Its answer is that the eloquence of the Qur'an is not for the sake of observing such constraints, but for the sake of the strength of its meanings and the sublimity of its words.

Know that when He rebuked them for worshipping other than God, He explicitly affirmed monotheism and denied partners, saying: ﴿God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾. There are several discussions here:

*The first:* We have explained in this book how the origination of human beings indicates the existence of the Creator who chooses, and how it indicates His oneness and His freedom from equals and rivals. So there is no benefit in repeating it.

*The second:* Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited ﴿God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers﴾ entirely in the accusative case (naṣb), as a substitution (badal) for "the Best of Creators." The rest recited it in the nominative case (raf'), as a new sentence (isti'naf). The first is the preference of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. The author of al-Kashshaf reported that Hamzah, when he connects the words, uses the accusative, and when he pauses, uses the nominative.

When God related that he had established monotheism with his people, He said: ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth﴾, that is, they will surely be brought forth to the Fire tomorrow. We have already discussed this at His words: ﴿you would surely have been among those brought forth﴾ (al-Saffat 37:57). Then God the Exalted says: ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾. This is because his people did not deny him entirely; rather, among them were some who had previously affirmed monotheism. Therefore God says: ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾, meaning those who came with pure monotheism, for they will not be brought forth.

Then He says: ﴿And We left for him a good name among later generations﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon the family of Yasin."﴾

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub recited "Al Yasin" (آلِ ياسِينَ) with the word āl (family) in construct with Yasin. The rest recited it with a kasra on the alif and a sukun on the lam, joined to Yasin (إلْ ياسِينَ).

As for the first recitation, there are several explanations:

The first, which is the closest: We have mentioned that he is Ilyas ibn Yasin, so Ilyas is the "family of Yasin."

The second: "The family of Yasin" means the family of Muhammad ﷺ.

The third: Yasin is a name of the Qur'an, as if it were said: "Peace of God be upon those who believe in the Book of God, which is Yasin." The first explanation is the most correct, because it best fits the context of the discourse.

As for the second recitation, there are several explanations:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: It is said "Mikal," "Mika'il," and "Mika'ilin," so similarly here "Ilyas" and "Ilyasin."

The second: al-Farra' said: It is a plural, and by it he intended Ilyas and his followers among the believers, like the phrases "al-Muhallabun" and "al-Sa'dun." He said:

*"I am the son of Sa'd, the most noble of the Sa'ds."*

Then God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ Its explanation has already preceded. And God knows best.

**The Second Issue:** There are two opinions concerning Ilyas. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "Wa inna Idris" (وإنَّ إدْرِيسَ) and said that Ilyas is Idris. This is also the view of 'Ikrimah. However, most commentators agree that he was a prophet from among the prophets of the Children of Israel, and that he is Ilyas ibn Yasin, from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both.

Then God the Exalted says: ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear God?"﴾ The implied meaning is: "Mention, O Muhammad, to your people: when he said to his people, 'Will you not fear God?'" That is, "Will you not fear God?" Al-Kalbi said: "Will you not fear the worship of other than God?"

Know that when he first warned them in general terms, he then mentioned the cause of that fear, saying: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators﴾. There are several points here:

*The first point:* Concerning "Ba'l" (بَعْلٍ) there are two opinions:

The first is that it is the proper name of an idol that they had, like Manat and Hubal. It is said that it was made of gold, that its height was twenty cubits, and that it had four faces. They were enamored with it and glorified it so much that they appointed four hundred attendants for it and made them prophets. The devil would enter the belly of Ba'l and speak the law of error, and the attendants would memorize it and teach it to the people. They were the people of Ba'labakk in the lands of Syria, and their city was named after it, Ba'labakk. Know that their saying that Ba'l is the name of one of their idols is not objectionable. But their claim that the devil used to enter the belly of Ba'labakk and speak the law of error is problematic. For if we permit this, it would cast doubt on many of the miracles, since it is reported in the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ that a wolf spoke to him, a camel spoke to him, and a trunk (of a palm tree) moaned. If we allowed that the devil could enter the body of a creature and speak, then this possibility would also exist for the wolf, the camel, and the trunk, and that would undermine their being miracles.

The second opinion: Ba'l means "the Lord" in the language of Yemen. It is said, "Who is the ba'l of this house?" meaning, "Who is its lord?" The husband is called ba'l in this sense. God the Exalted says: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:228), and He says: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ (Hud 11:72). According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "Do you worship some lord other than God and abandon the worship of God?"

*The second point:* The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) used this verse to argue that the servant creates his own actions. They said: If no one other than God were a creator, it would not be permissible to describe God as "the Best of Creators." The discussion of this has already been presented in His words: ﴿So blessed is God, the Best of Creators﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:14).

*The third point:* The one known as al-Rashid al-Katib used to say: "If it were said, 'Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators,' it would give the impression that [Ba'l] is the best, because there would be an observance of the sense of embellishment." Its answer is that the eloquence of the Qur'an is not for the sake of observing such constraints, but for the sake of the strength of its meanings and the sublimity of its words.

Know that when He rebuked them for worshipping other than God, He explicitly affirmed monotheism and denied partners, saying: ﴿God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾. There are several discussions here:

*The first:* We have explained in this book how the origination of human beings indicates the existence of the Creator who chooses, and how it indicates His oneness and His freedom from equals and rivals. So there is no benefit in repeating it.

*The second:* Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim recited ﴿God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers﴾ entirely in the accusative case (naṣb), as a substitution (badal) for "the Best of Creators." The rest recited it in the nominative case (raf'), as a new sentence (isti'naf). The first is the preference of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd. The author of al-Kashshaf reported that Hamzah, when he connects the words, uses the accusative, and when he pauses, uses the nominative.

When God related that he had established monotheism with his people, He said: ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth﴾, that is, they will surely be brought forth to the Fire tomorrow. We have already discussed this at His words: ﴿you would surely have been among those brought forth﴾ (al-Saffat 37:57). Then God the Exalted says: ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾. This is because his people did not deny him entirely; rather, among them were some who had previously affirmed monotheism. Therefore God says: ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾, meaning those who came with pure monotheism, for they will not be brought forth.

Then He says: ﴿And We left for him a good name among later generations﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon the family of Yasin."﴾

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub recited "Al Yasin" (آلِ ياسِينَ) with the word āl (family) in construct with Yasin. The rest recited it with a kasra on the alif and a sukun on the lam, joined to Yasin (إلْ ياسِينَ).

As for the first recitation, there are several explanations:

The first, which is the closest: We have mentioned that he is Ilyas ibn Yasin, so Ilyas is the "family of Yasin."

The second: "The family of Yasin" means the family of Muhammad ﷺ.

The third: Yasin is a name of the Qur'an, as if it were said: "Peace of God be upon those who believe in the Book of God, which is Yasin." The first explanation is the most correct, because it best fits the context of the discourse.

As for the second recitation, there are several explanations:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: It is said "Mikal," "Mika'il," and "Mika'ilin," so similarly here "Ilyas" and "Ilyasin."

The second: al-Farra' said: It is a plural, and by it he intended Ilyas and his followers among the believers, like the phrases "al-Muhallabun" and "al-Sa'dun." He said:

*"I am the son of Sa'd, the most noble of the Sa'ds."*

Then God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ Its explanation has already preceded. And God knows best.

The Story of Lot, peace be upon him

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers﴾ ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them﴾ ﴿Except an old woman among those who remained behind﴾ ﴿Then We destroyed the others﴾ ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ ﴿And at night. Will you not then use reason?﴾

This is the fifth story. Allah the Exalted mentioned this story so that the polytheists of the Arabs might take a lesson from it, for those of his people who disbelieved were destroyed, and those who believed were saved. The explanation of this story has already been given before. He alerted them with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ ﴿and at night﴾. This is because the people used to travel to Syria, and the traveler, for the most part, journeys at night and at the beginning of the day. For this reason, Allah the Exalted specified these two times.

* * *

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾, meaning: Do you not have minds by which you might take heed? And Allah knows best.

The Story of Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers. When he fled to the laden ship. And he drew lots and was among the losers. Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy. And had he not been of those who glorify Allah. He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected. So We cast him onto the open shore while he was ailing. And We caused to grow over him a gourd plant. And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more. And they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time.﴾

Know that this is the sixth story and the last of the stories mentioned in this surah. This story came to be the conclusion of the stories because, when he did not endure the harm of his people and fled to the ship, he fell into those hardships. This serves as an example for the Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient with the harm of his people.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers. When he fled to the laden ship﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read "Yunus" with a damma and a kasra on the nun.

The second issue: This verse indicates that this event happened to Yunus (peace be upon him) after he had become a messenger, because His saying: ﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers. When he fled to the ship﴾ means that he was among the messengers at the time he fled to the ship. It may be said: many narrations report that the king of his time sent him to those people to call them to Allah, then he fled and the fish swallowed him, and at that point Allah sent him. The conclusion is that His saying ﴿among the messengers﴾ does not indicate that at that time he was a messenger from Allah the Exalted. It may be answered that He, glory be to Him, mentioned this description in the context of honouring him, and it would not convey this benefit unless the meaning of His saying ﴿among the messengers﴾ is that he was among the messengers in the sight of Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: "Abaqa" (fled) derives from the fleeing of a slave, which is his running away from his master. Then the exegetes differed. Some said: he fled from Allah the Exalted, and this is far-fetched, because that is only said of one who deliberately opposes his Lord, and that is not permissible for the prophets. They differed regarding why he became mistaken. It was said: because he was commanded to go out to the Children of Israel, but he did not accept that duty and went out angry at his Lord. This is far-fetched, whether Allah commanded him with that by revelation or through the tongue of another prophet. It was also said: his sin was that he abandoned calling his people and did not endure patiently with them. This too is far-fetched, because when Allah the Exalted commanded him with this task, it is not permissible for him to abandon it. The closest view in this regard has two aspects:

The first: his sin was that Allah the Exalted had promised him the sending down of destruction upon his people who denied him, so he thought it would certainly descend. Because of this assumption he did not endure patiently with calling them, and it was obligatory upon him to persist in calling them, since it was possible that Allah would not destroy them with the punishment even if He sent it down. This is the closest view, because it is an undertaking of a matter whose signs had appeared, so it is not a deliberate act of disobedience. Although the better course in such matters is not to act upon assumption. Then it became clear to Yunus afterwards that he had erred in that assumption, because faith appeared among them. So the meaning of His saying ﴿When he fled to the ship﴾ is what we have mentioned.

The second aspect: Yunus had promised his people the punishment, and when the punishment was delayed from them, he went out as one hidden from them, intending the sea and boarding the ship. That is His saying ﴿When he fled to the ship﴾. The full discussion of the difficulties of this verse we have mentioned in His saying: ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree against him﴾ (al-Anbiya: 87). As for His saying ﴿to the laden ship﴾, it is explained in Surah Yunus. A ship in which there is a great load and people is said to be laden (mashhun). Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿fasahama﴾. Al-musahama is al-muqara'a (casting lots). It is said: "asham al-qawm" when they drew lots. Al-Mubarrad said: it is taken from the arrows (sihām) which are shuffled for the lottery. ﴿and was among the losers﴾, i.e., the defeated. It is said: "adhda'a Allahu hujjatahu," so it was "duhida" (refuted), meaning He removed it and it was removed. The root of the word is from al-dahd, which is slipperiness. It is said: "dahadat rijlu al-ba'ir" when the camel's foot slipped.

Ibn 'Abbas mentioned in the story of Yunus (peace be upon him) that he used to live with his people in Filastin (Palestine). A king invaded them and took captive from them nine and a half tribes, and two and a half tribes remained. Allah the Exalted had revealed to the Children of Israel: "If your enemy takes you captive, or a calamity befalls you, call upon Me and I will answer you." But when they forgot that and were taken captive, Allah the Exalted after a time revealed to one of their prophets: "Go to the king of these peoples and say to him: until he sends to the Children of Israel a prophet." So Yunus (peace be upon him) was chosen for his strength and trustworthiness. Yunus said: "Did Allah command you with this?" He said: "No, but I was commanded to send a strong and trustworthy man, and you are such." Yunus said: "Among the Children of Israel there is one stronger than me, so why do you not send him?" The king insisted upon him, and Yunus became angry with him, and went out until he came to the Sea of Rum, and found a ship laden, and they carried him in it. When it entered the depths of the sea, it came close to sinking. The sailors said: "Among you there is a disobedient one, otherwise there would not have happened in the ship what we see without wind or apparent cause." The merchants said: "We have tried the like of this before. When we see him, we will draw lots, and whoever's lot comes out, we will throw him into the sea, for one person drowning is better than all drowning." The lot of Yunus came out. The merchants said: "We are more deserving of the sin than the prophet of Allah." Then they returned a second and third time, casting lots, and the lot of Yunus came out. He said: "O people, I am the disobedient one," and he wrapped himself in a cloak and threw himself down, and the fish swallowed him. Allah the Exalted revealed to the fish: "Do not break any bone of his, nor cut any joint of his." Then the fish brought him out to the Nile of Egypt, then to the Sea of Persia, then to the Sea of al-Bata'ih, then the Tigris, and it ascended with him and cast him on the land of Nasibin, in the open, and he was like a plucked fledgling, with no hair and no flesh. Allah caused to grow over him a gourd plant, and he would shade himself beneath it and eat from its fruit until he grew strong. Then the earth consumed it and it fell from its root. Yunus grieved over that a great grief, and said: "O Lord, I used to shade myself beneath this tree from the sun and the wind, and suck from its fruit, and now it has fallen." It was said to him: "O Yunus, you grieve over a tree that was grown in an hour and uprooted in an hour, and you do not grieve over a hundred thousand or more whom you abandoned! Go to them." And Allah knows best the reality of the event.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ It is said: "iltaqamahu" and "iltahamahu," both with the same meaning. His saying ﴿and he was blameworthy﴾: it is said "alama" when one commits what deserves blame. So al-mulim is one who deserves blame, who has committed what is blameworthy.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had he not been of those who glorify Allah. He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ Regarding the explanation of his being among those who glorify, there are two views:

The first: what is meant is what Allah the Exalted related of him in another verse, that he was saying in those darknesses: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾.

The second: that had he not been, before the fish swallowed him, among those who glorify, that is, those who pray, and had he not been constant in most times in the remembrance of Allah and His obedience, he would have remained in the belly of that fish, and its belly would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. Some of them said: remember Allah in ease and He will remember you in hardship, for Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant, mindful of Allah the Exalted, so when he fell into the belly of the fish, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And had he not been of those who glorify Allah. He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ And Pharaoh was a tyrannical, forgetful servant, so when drowning overtook him he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾ [Yunus: 90]. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before﴾ [Yunus: 91].

They differed about how long he remained in the belly of the fish, and the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate it. al-Hasan said: he remained only a short while, and he was brought out from its belly after the time when it had swallowed him. From Muqatil ibn Hayyan: three days. From 'Ata': seven days. From al-Dahhak: twenty days. It was also said: a month. I do not know by what evidence they specified these measures.

From Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Yunus glorified Allah in the belly of the fish, and the angels heard his glorification, and they said: 'Our Lord, we hear a weak voice in a strange land.' He said: 'That is My servant Yunus, who disobeyed Me, so I imprisoned him in the belly of the fish in the sea.' They said: 'The righteous servant from whom a righteous deed used to ascend to You every day and night?' He said: 'Yes.' So they interceded for him, and He commanded the fish, and it cast him onto the shore." That is His saying: ﴿So We cast him onto the open shore﴾. And in this are several discussions:

The first: al-'ara' is the empty place. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it was called "al-'ara'" only because there is no tree in it and nothing covers it.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We cast him onto the open shore﴾, attributing that casting to Himself, while the casting actually occurred through the action of the fish. This indicates that the act of the servant is created by Allah the Exalted.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while he was ailing﴾. It was said: what is meant is that his flesh had decayed and he became weak like a newborn child, like a fledgling plucked of its feathers, having no down. Mujahid said: "saqim" means "salib" (deprived of strength).

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd plant﴾. The apparent wording indicates that when the fish cast him onto the open shore, Allah the Exalted caused to grow over him a gourd plant, and that was a miracle for him. Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: every plant that does not stand on a stalk but spreads over the surface of the earth is "yaqtin," such as the squash, the colocynth, and the watermelon. Al-Zajjaj said: I think its derivation is from "qatana bi-al-makan" when he stayed in a place, and this plant's leaves all lie on the surface of the earth, so it was called yaqtin. Al-Farra' related that it was said in the presence of Ibn 'Abbas that it was the leaves of the pumpkin. He said: whoever makes the pumpkin among the trees a yaqtin... every leaf that spreads and provides cover is a yaqtin. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the verse implies two things that the exegetes did not mention:

One: that this yaqtin did not exist before, and Allah caused it to grow for his sake.

The other: that the yaqtin was trellised so that he would have shade, for if it had spread flat on the ground he would not have been able to shade himself beneath it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾. In this there are several discussions:

The first: it is possible that what is meant is that We sent him before the fish swallowed him, and although this sending is mentioned after the swallowing, what is meant is precedence, and the conjunction "wa" means gathering. It is also possible that what is meant is the sending after the swallowing. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the mission of Yunus (peace be upon him) was after the fish cast him out. On this reckoning it is permissible that he was sent to a people other than the first people, and it is permissible that he was sent again to the first people with a law, and they believed in it.

The second discussion: the apparent wording of His saying ﴿or more﴾ implies doubt, and that is impossible for Allah the Exalted. Its parallels are His saying: ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ [al-Mursalat: 6], His saying: ﴿so that he may remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], His saying: ﴿so that they may fear Him or He may bring about for them a reminder﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113], His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye or even nearer﴾ [al-Nahl: 77], and His saying: ﴿And he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9]. They answered this in many ways, and the most correct of them is one way: that the meaning is "or they exceed in your estimation," in the sense that when the observer sees them he says: these are a hundred thousand or more beyond the hundred. This is the answer for everything resembling this.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they believed, and We let them enjoy [their lives] for a time.﴾ The meaning is that when those peoples believed, God removed the fear from them, secured them from the punishment, and God let them enjoy [worldly life] until a time, that is, until the appointed term that God set as the lifespan of each one of them.
